Katalog Berita (Halaman 31/57)

#5341. OpenAI pushes forward with AMD partnership amid ongoing efforts to diversify from Nvidia

Welcome to Eye on AI. Emily Forlini here, filling in for Jeremy Kahn. In today’s issue:

Before we get to the news, can I just say, you are not going to want to miss this year’s edition of Fortune Brainstorm AI San Francisco.

We have an exceptional lineup of speakers for you: OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman will both be onstage. Once the closest of partners, their two companies are increasingly competitors, so I’m eager to hear how differently they see the road ahead. AI pioneers Fei-Fei Li, now of World Labs, as well as Andrew Ng, now of LearnVector, will be discussing their view of AI’s future too. Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora will talk about AI and cybersecurity. Greylock partner Reid Hoffman, CapitalG’s Jill Chase, and Kleiner Perkins’ Mamoon Hamid and Ilya Fushman will weigh in on where the money is going. Recursive Superintelligence’s Richard Socher will talk about RSI and automating AI research.

It’s going to be epic. So please join me and many of my Fortune colleagues at the St. Regis in San Francisco on Dec. 7 and 8. You can apply to attend here.

Long before Jensen Huang resigned, the major AI companies were already building toward a world where he was less central to their success. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have been acutely aware of their dependence on Nvidia hardware, given that much of the AI ecosystem is built on it, and have ongoing efforts to diversify their infrastructure.

OpenAI is particularly vulnerable to any disruption in Nvidia’s business. Its models run almost entirely on Nvidia GPUs, a source familiar with its compute infrastructure tells me. Its CEO Sam Altman said this week that it would be “hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen” when speaking at a Semafor conference.

Meanwhile, Anthropic has a more diversified chip base. It relies on four main providers: Google TPUs, AMD GPUs, Amazon Trainium GPUs, and Nvidia GPUs, its S-1 revealed. This is a major competitive advantage, and Anthropic has built a “proprietary orchestration layer” that optimizes which workloads run on which chips, reducing its costs.

OpenAI has been focused on replicating this setup through a few initiatives. For one, it’s designing its own chip architecture, called Jalapeño. It’s also signing deals with non-Nvidia suppliers. OpenAI is reportedly planning to buy Google’s TPU chips, and this week, it announced a big step forward in a massive compute deal it signed with AMD in October to provide 6 gigawatts of capacity. For context, that’s five times the capacity of OpenAI’s flagship data center in Abilene, Texas, which has 1.2 gigawatts, and is one of the world’s largest campuses.

(AMD is curiously run by Jensen Huang’s first cousin once removed, Lisa Su. One source tells me Su’s least favorite question from reporters is about them being cousins; she hasn’t made it a part of her public image.)

OpenAI revealed the first neocloud company associated with the AMD deal, called TensorWave. TensorWave will provide OpenAI with 457 megawatts of capacity across multiple U.S. data center sites. That’s just 7.6% of the total capacity involved in the AMD deal. However, it’s TensorWave’s largest deployment ever, and the company will need to roughly triple its staff to support it, a company spokesperson tells me.

Why announce this now? The timing might seem a bit opportunistic given the turmoil at Nvidia, but a TensorWave spokesperson tells me it had been trying to determine the timing of this announcement for a while. It wasn’t sure now was the right time given Huang’s resignation, but it decided to move forward in light of this week’s Supercomputing 2026 conference, which is “one of the last major compute conferences of the year.” The company wanted to get the news out “ASAP since there will be a lot of great people attending, a lot of great opportunities to meet with potential hires.” (Nvidia also has a booth.)

The first gigawatt of capacity from the OpenAI-AMD deal is set to come online in the second half of this year. The TensorWave capacity will follow, expected in the first half of 2027, with the full deployment expected by early 2028. Meanwhile, OpenAI’s proprietary Jalapeño chip, developed in partnership with Broadcom, is set to scale up production in 2027.

OpenAI’s plan is to become less Nvidia reliant over time. But it would still be ideal for Altman if Huang came back to preserve stability. And Huang is already trying to do just that. Today, he hard launched his comeback campaign, posting on X that he would be “honored” to return as CEO.

For now, Huang’s return is looking unlikely. Sources tell me the Nvidia board is already working with multiple search firms to find his replacement, and the board told CNBC it is not considering bringing Huang back. Investigations into any foul play, specifically selling chips to China, are also underway. The board has created an oversight committee to ensure compliance with U.S. export controls, and Huang has agreed to appear before the House in a closed-door hearing on on Dec. 1.

But Huang, who is considered almost God-like in some AI circles—as my colleagues Beatrice Nolan and Jeremy Kahn wrote in this excellent piece for the Fortune print magazine—could surprise us.

With that, here’s more AI news.Emily Forliniemily.forlini@fortune.com@emilyforlini

Finally, just a reminder to check out the latest episode of our vodcast, Fortune AI Weekly, here on YouTube.

Isomorphic Labs has raised a $5 billion Series C for AI-powered drug discovery. Former Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis' company tells me the funding will accelerate its efforts to find new drugs. Some of its most advanced projects are focused on treatments for cancer and malaria. The money will go toward expanding its proprietary AI models, scaling up its infrastructure, widening its partner portfolio, and more. Read more here from Isomorphic Labs.

California Attorney General sues OpenAI over the Hugging Face breach. Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of developing its products without adequate safety procedures, and fostering a company culture that prioritizes speed over safety, thus endangering the public. The suit follows another from Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who last month sued OpenAI—and Sam Altman himself—for allegedly endangering its users, primarily children. OpenAI also faces a lawsuit filed by eight states over its alleged harming of young users, as well as over 30 lawsuits filed in relation to a school shooting in Canada. Read more here in Reuters.

OpenAI grants access to four third-party safety organizations to inspect its models. In a key step to improve its processes, especially since the Hugging Face hack, OpenAI has invited outside researchers into its offices, giving them special access to its most advanced models. Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire will assess problematic behaviors such as subversion and scheming, as well as the effectiveness of OpenAI's safeguards over an extended period. Read more here from Quartz.

Google identifies a threat actor using AI to autonomously exploit vulnerabilities in the wild. An LLM framework called exploit_agent, which was configured with Russian-language tooling, could identify vulnerabilities and automatically develop exploits without human intervention. Google says it's the first time such a discovery has been made, and the wider adoption of agentic tools by bad actors has "crossed a significant threshold."  Read more here from Google.

Always-on AI agents struggle to finish tasks without intervention. A team of researchers at Microsoft set up a simulated workplace to see how AI agents would perform at finding and completing tasks without being asked. They say current model benchmarks only evaluate how well agents complete tasks explicitly given to them. But what if the AI has to identify tasks on its own, and then complete them, without humans involved?

The team unleashed the models on the simulated workplace—complete with fake employees, projects, business systems, and historical events—and, it turns out, they're not very good. The study found varying breakdowns for different models. The weaker ones were the worst at discovering tasks. The intermediate models were better at identifying tasks, but often stopped short of carrying them out. The strongest models also often failed mainly during execution.

Maybe our jobs are safe, for now. Read the full study here.

Dec. 6-12: Neural Information Processing Systems (Neurips) conference. Sydney, Australia.

Dec. 7-8: Fortune Brainstorm AI, San Francisco. Apply here to attend.

AI-powered houseplants can now shame you for not watering them. A Carnegie Mellon PhD student created a small gadget that sits next to any object, such as a plant, and brings it to life. The display shows a cute AI avatar, called an Object Agent Twin (OAT), that reacts on the object's behalf. For example, if the plant's leaves are yellow and you haven't watered recently, the OAT will look sad and dejected. When you add water, it becomes visibly excited and happy. As Wired puts it, the AI is turning everyday objects into needy virtual pets.

#5340. What flood insurance covers, what FEMA aid covers and where they differ

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Flood insurance vs. FEMA disaster aid comes down to coverage, eligibility and repayment rules, and these 10 slides explain what each pays for and where gaps remain

A flood insurance policy is a contract bought before the water rises. FEMA disaster aid is a federal program that switches on only after the president declares a major disaster. That single difference shapes how each one pays, who qualifies and how much a household can expect to recover.

A standard homeowners policy does not settle the question. Those policies, along with renters insurance, exclude flood damage. After a flood, that leaves two main places to look for money: a separate flood policy, or federal assistance if the event is declared. The two are built for different jobs.

Flood insurance pays defined limits under the terms of the policy, whether or not a disaster declaration follows. FEMA's individual assistance has a narrower purpose. It is meant to cover basic needs and support recovery. It is not designed to return a home to the condition it was in before the flood. Most of that help comes as grants that generally do not have to be repaid.

Putting flood insurance vs FEMA disaster aid side by side shows where each one fills a gap and where neither does. A flood policy leaves out some costs, such as temporary lodging. Federal aid may never arrive if a flood is not declared a major disaster. Each source also runs on its own clock, with separate waiting periods, filing windows and deadlines.

The 10 slides that follow start with how the National Flood Insurance Program works, what a standard policy pays for and what it excludes. They then turn to FEMA's Individuals and Households Program, what its grants cover and when that help becomes available. Later slides explain why homeowners policies exclude flood, who is required to buy coverage, how the two sources interact and how to apply for each.

Each slide stands on its own. A reader can go straight to one question, such as whether FEMA pays for flood damage or what flood insurance covers. Others answer whether homeowners insurance covers floods and what happens when a household has both.

The National Flood Insurance Program is a federal flood insurance program created by Congress in the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968. FEMA administers it, while insurance companies and agents sell the policies and the federal program stands behind them.

A buyer usually works with an insurance agent or company rather than a government office. Under FEMA's Write Your Own program, private insurers sell and service NFIP policies under their own company names. Policies can also be bought through NFIP Direct, which sells and services coverage on the program's behalf. Either way, the quote, the premium bill and the policy documents arrive through that channel.

NFIP coverage is sold only in communities that participate in the program. To join, a community agrees to adopt and enforce floodplain management rules meant to reduce future flood damage. A homeowner, renter or business owner in a participating community can buy a policy. That holds whether or not the property sits in a mapped high-risk zone.

An NFIP policy is a contract. The buyer pays a premium up front. In return, the policy promises to pay for covered flood losses up to limits written into it. Those terms are set when the policy is issued. The policyholder knows the ceiling for each type of coverage at the time of purchase.

A standard National Flood Insurance Program policy for a single-family home pays up to $250,000 for the building and up to $100,000 for contents. These are two separate coverages. Each one carries its own limit.

Those figures are program maximums, not fixed amounts. A policyholder can choose lower coverage amounts. The line between building and contents coverage is the first thing to understand about any flood claim.

Building coverage applies to the physical house. It covers the structure itself and the foundation it rests on. It also covers the electrical and plumbing systems that run through the home. Furnaces and water heaters fall under the building side as well.

Contents coverage works differently. It is a separate purchase, not an automatic part of every flood policy. A homeowner who buys only building coverage has no flood protection for belongings. Contents coverage pays for personal property such as clothing and furniture.

FEMA's Individuals and Households Program gives direct help to people affected by a declared disaster. That help comes mostly as grants, which generally do not have to be repaid.

The program sets a narrow goal. It covers basic needs and helps a household take the first steps toward recovery. Making a damaged home whole again falls outside its purpose.

Its name describes who it serves. Money and help go to individuals and households, not to businesses or local governments. Applicants deal directly with FEMA, the same federal agency that administers the National Flood Insurance Program. The agency runs the two under separate rules, and an aid application is not an insurance claim.

The grant structure shapes a household's finances after a flood. A grant generally carries no obligation to pay the money back. A loan, by contrast, adds debt at the moment a family is trying to recover. A grant also differs from insurance in another way. No one pays a premium in advance to qualify.

FEMA aid for individuals and households becomes available only after the president issues a major disaster declaration. A flood that never receives one brings no direct federal assistance to homeowners or renters, however much damage it causes.

The authority for this system comes from the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act, signed into law in 1988. The Stafford Act governs how federal disaster help flows to states, local governments and individuals. It puts the decision to declare a major disaster in the president's hands, not FEMA's.

The request normally starts with a governor. When a storm or flood causes damage beyond what state and local governments can manage, the governor asks the president for a declaration. Tribal governments can also request declarations directly.

Federal law requires flood insurance for a building in a Special Flood Hazard Area that carries a federally backed mortgage. The requirement is tied to the loan, and the lender enforces it.

A Special Flood Hazard Area is land that FEMA maps as having at least a 1% chance of flooding in any given year. These zones appear on Flood Insurance Rate Maps. Their labels begin with the letter A or V.

The mandate dates to the Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973. It reaches mortgages from federally regulated or insured lenders. It also covers loans insured or guaranteed by federal agencies such as the FHA and the VA.

The mortgage is the trigger, not the flood zone alone. An owner in a Special Flood Hazard Area with no federally backed mortgage falls outside this federal mandate. That owner decides whether to buy flood coverage.

A new National Flood Insurance Program policy generally takes effect only after a 30-day waiting period. FEMA disaster aid follows a different timeline. Its application window opens with a disaster declaration and closes on a deadline that the declaration sets.

The waiting period decides whether a policy can help with a given flood. A policy bought as a storm approaches generally will not pay for damage from that storm. Coverage has to be in force before the water arrives.

The 30-day rule has exceptions. One involves some loan closings, where flood insurance bought in connection with the loan can start without the full wait. A homeowner with no loan transaction underway generally faces the standard 30 days.

Once a flood has damaged an insured property, the claim goes to the insurer that issued the policy. That holds whether the coverage came through the NFIP or a private company. The insurer handles the claim, not FEMA's disaster aid program.

A covered loss leads to a claim because the policyholder bought coverage. The insurer pays under the policy's terms, and no government declaration is needed to trigger that payment. Federal disaster aid works on a separate track, with its own eligibility rules and no advance promise of a specific dollar amount.

FEMA's dual role can blur the line. The agency administers the NFIP and also runs federal disaster assistance for individuals and households. The two remain separate programs. One is coverage a person pays for in advance. The other is help the government provides on its own conditions.

The split matters for renters too. A tenant does not own the structure. Building coverage does nothing for them. Renters can buy contents coverage on its own to protect what they keep inside a rented home.

Each coverage has its own deductible. A flood that damages both the house and the belongings inside it can mean two deductibles on one claim. Contents are generally paid at actual cash value. That figure reflects depreciation. It is usually lower than the cost of buying the same items new.

Limits are higher for non-residential buildings, such as a business property. A non-residential building can carry up to $500,000 in building coverage. It can carry a further $500,000 in contents coverage.

The NFIP also includes Increased Cost of Compliance coverage. A substantially damaged building may have to meet local floodplain rules before it can be rebuilt. Increased Cost of Compliance pays up to $30,000 toward meeting those rules after a covered loss. The money can go toward elevating the building, floodproofing it, relocating it or demolishing it.

Every limit here is a ceiling rather than a promised payout. A claim pays the documented loss, minus the deductible, up to the amount of coverage bought.

A National Flood Insurance Program policy does not pay additional living expenses, such as a hotel stay while a flooded home is repaired. It also excludes business interruption, vehicles, outdoor landscaping, and money and valuable papers. Coverage in a basement is sharply limited.

The missing living-expense coverage affects any household forced out during repairs. A standard homeowners policy often includes loss-of-use coverage for the perils it covers. An NFIP policy has no equivalent. A household that cannot stay in its home pays for rent, hotels and meals from its own savings or from other sources.

Business interruption is excluded in the same way. An NFIP policy on a commercial building can pay to repair the structure and replace contents within its limits. It does not replace the income a business loses while its doors are closed for cleanup and repairs.

Vehicles sit outside flood insurance entirely. A car swamped in a driveway, street or garage is a matter for an auto policy. Comprehensive auto coverage generally pays for flood damage. A liability-only auto policy does not.

Most property outside the walls of the building is also excluded. Lawns, trees and shrubs are not covered. Neither are fences, swimming pools, patios, walkways or driveways.

Certain valuables are left out of contents coverage as well. Cash, precious metals and valuable papers such as stock certificates are not covered, even when they are inside the insured home.

The NFIP defines a basement as any area of a building with its floor below ground level on all sides. Coverage there is limited to essentials. Building coverage pays for mechanical equipment such as furnaces, water heaters, central air conditioners, sump pumps and electrical panels.

Contents coverage, if the owner bought it, extends only to a short list of basement items, such as washers, dryers and food freezers. Finished walls, floors and ceilings are not covered. Carpet and most belongings stored below ground are not covered either.

As a result, a finished basement used as a family room or guest space can flood and leave most of its finishes and furnishings unpaid. The policy also does not pay for mold or mildew damage that results from an owner failing to inspect and maintain the property after floodwater recedes.

The program does have eligibility conditions. At least one member of the household must be a U.S. citizen, a non-citizen national or a qualified noncitizen. The help is tied to a primary residence. A vacation home or other secondary property does not qualify.

The amount of help is also limited. Federal law caps what a household can receive through the program, and those caps are adjusted each year for inflation.

FEMA disaster assistance is not counted as taxable income. It also does not affect eligibility for public benefits such as Social Security or Medicaid.

For a flooded household, the practical result is a gap between what the program provides and what a full repair costs. Grants aimed at essentials can carry a family through the weeks after a flood. Rebuilding a home to its former condition depends on other sources, such as an insurance payout or savings.

FEMA's Individuals and Households Program pays for two broad categories of need: Housing Assistance and Other Needs Assistance. The first deals with where a household lives after a disaster, while the second covers serious disaster-caused costs beyond the home itself.

Housing Assistance has three main uses. It can pay for temporary housing when a home cannot be lived in. It can pay for repairs to a damaged home. In limited cases, it can help pay to replace a home that was destroyed.

Temporary housing help can take more than one form. FEMA can provide money to rent another place to live while the household is displaced. In some disasters, it also provides direct housing, such as a manufactured housing unit placed near the damaged property.

Repair help has a defined target. It is meant to make a primary home safe, sanitary and functional again. It is not meant to cover upgrades or cosmetic work. A homeowner can receive repair money and still have work left to finish.

Other Needs Assistance covers a separate set of expenses. Medical and dental costs caused by the disaster fall into this category. So do funeral costs and transportation costs. Some personal property is eligible as well.

These costs have nothing to do with a building's structure. An injury during an evacuation can lead to medical bills. A death in the family can bring funeral expenses. A car ruined by floodwater can leave a worker with no way to reach a job. Transportation help can cover repair or replacement of a disaster-damaged vehicle when the household has no other usable one.

The personal property piece is narrower than the phrase suggests. It generally reaches essential household items, such as basic furniture, appliances and clothing. It does not aim to replace everything a household owned.

Each category is tied to a need the disaster created. Costs the disaster did not cause fall outside both parts of the program.

Before that request is made, state, local and federal officials typically carry out preliminary damage assessments. These surveys document how many homes were damaged, how badly and how many lacked insurance. The governor's request draws on those findings.

Not every flood reaches that stage. Localized flooding from a single heavy storm can cause serious losses to individual households without prompting a declaration request.

A declaration also does not cover every area touched by the same disaster. Each one lists the specific counties, or equivalent areas such as Louisiana parishes, that qualify. It also states which types of help apply in each place.

Individual assistance may be approved for some counties while others receive only public assistance. Public assistance reimburses governments and certain nonprofits for work such as debris removal and repairs to roads and public buildings. A household in a county approved only for public assistance cannot apply for individual aid under that declaration.

The list of counties can change. FEMA can amend a declaration to add counties or types of help as more damage assessments come in. A declaration may also arrive days or weeks after floodwaters recede, depending on how long the assessments and review take.

Standard homeowners and renters insurance policies do not pay for flood damage. Protection against rising or overflowing water requires a separate flood policy, bought through the National Flood Insurance Program or from a private insurer.

The exclusion turns on where the water comes from. Homeowners and renters policies treat flood as water that rises from the ground up. That includes surface water that collects and spreads across land. It also includes water that spills over from a river, lake or the sea. If that water enters a home, a homeowners or renters policy does not pay for the damage.

The NFIP uses its own detailed definition. Its standard policy describes a flood as a general and temporary condition in which normally dry land is partly or completely inundated. The event has to cover two or more acres of land or two or more properties. At least one of those properties must be the policyholder's. Overflow of inland or tidal waters qualifies. So does an unusual and rapid buildup or runoff of surface water, and so does mudflow.

Water that arrives from above is often handled differently. When wind damages a roof and rain gets in through the opening, a homeowners policy may cover the resulting harm. That outcome is not automatic. Wording varies from one policy and insurer to the next. The specific terms of each policy determine where the line falls.

Water that backs up through drains or sewer lines is another separate category. Many homeowners policies exclude it unless the owner adds a water backup endorsement. That endorsement is not flood coverage, and it does not replace a flood policy.

For renters, the gap applies to belongings rather than the building. The landlord's insurance covers the structure, not a tenant's possessions. A renters policy protects those possessions against many risks, but it excludes flood. The NFIP sells contents-only flood policies that renters can buy to fill that gap.

A household with full homeowners or renters coverage can still have no insurance at all for a flood. A flood policy is a separate purchase from a homeowners policy. It carries its own premium, limits and terms.

Lenders check compliance when a loan is made and over its life. The required amount is generally the lowest of three figures: the outstanding loan balance, the building's insurable value or the maximum the NFIP offers. If a borrower lets required coverage lapse, the lender can buy a policy and charge the borrower for it. This is known as force-placed insurance.

The mandate does not have to be met with a National Flood Insurance Program policy. A private flood policy can satisfy it if the policy meets federal criteria. Rules from federal banking regulators that took effect in 2019 require lenders to accept private policies that meet those criteria.

Private limits, deductibles and terms vary from one insurer to the next. A buyer comparing options has to read each policy on its own terms.

The NFIP also changed how it prices its own policies, under a rating approach called Risk Rating 2.0. It applied to new policies from Oct. 1, 2021. It applied to all renewing policies from April 1, 2022.

Risk Rating 2.0 weighs the features of an individual property rather than relying mainly on its flood zone. FEMA lists factors such as distance to a water source, flood frequency, flood type and the cost to rebuild.

Federal law bars duplication of benefits. FEMA cannot pay for a loss that insurance already covers, so a flood policy and FEMA aid never pay for the same item.

The rule sets the order in which the two sources work. Insurance comes first for a covered loss. FEMA then looks only at the needs the insurance did not meet.

Having a flood insurance policy does not disqualify anyone from FEMA help. A policyholder can still apply for federal aid after a flood. FEMA judges the application against what the policy left uncovered, not against the full extent of the damage.

The size of a household's loss does not decide what FEMA pays. The gap between the loss and the insurance coverage is what counts. A household whose policy covered most of its damage may have little left for FEMA to address.

Insured applicants generally need to show FEMA how their claim turned out. FEMA typically asks for the insurance settlement or denial letter before deciding on aid for an insured loss. A denial or a settlement that falls short can open the door to federal help for the uncovered part.

The rule also works in reverse. If an insurance payment later covers something FEMA already paid for, the applicant may have to return that FEMA money.

FEMA also refers applicants to the Small Business Administration. The SBA offers low-interest disaster loans to homeowners and renters as well as businesses. Unlike most FEMA help, which comes as grants, these loans must be repaid.

That makes the three sources different in kind. An insurance claim pays under a contract bought in advance. A FEMA grant generally does not have to be repaid. An SBA disaster loan adds debt, even at a low rate.

The duplication rule keeps these sources from stacking on the same loss. Each payment has to answer a need the others did not meet.

An NFIP policyholder generally has to submit a proof of loss within 60 days of the loss. The proof of loss is the policyholder's own statement of the amount being claimed. Extensions are often granted.

FEMA aid follows a separate path. Applications go through DisasterAssistance.gov or by phone at 800-621-3362. Filing an insurance claim does not count as applying to FEMA. Applying to FEMA does not open an insurance claim.

FEMA application deadlines are not fixed nationally. Each disaster declaration sets its own. The declaration covering a household's county is where the applicable date appears.

A household with flood insurance in a declared area can end up facing two deadlines at once. The proof of loss deadline runs 60 days from the date of the loss. The FEMA deadline runs to whatever date the declaration sets. Meeting one deadline does not satisfy the other.

#5339. Uncommon Thinkers: Alexis Harroun aims for space with a new engine — and stays grounded

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:48 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

A few weeks after learning that her tiny startup had won a NASA prize to fly its engine in space, Alexis Harroun was camping in Yellowstone, sitting around a fire and looking up at the stars. Satellites kept drifting past overhead — and the news finally sank in.

“I’m like, oh, we’re going to be sending something up and we’re going to be able to see it,” she said. “That was very humbling in a lot of ways and very exciting.”

Harroun is co-founder and CEO of Juno Propulsion, a Tukwila, Wash.-based startup building a new kind of rocket engine. Instead of a steady flame, Juno’s engines use detonation, a supersonic combustion wave that releases more energy from the same amount of propellant.

“It’s essentially like a higher MPG rocket engine,” Harroun said.

The technology has been studied for decades but has never flown in orbit. Juno aims to change that next year, when its engine is set to fly aboard a Momentus satellite in a mission called Project Iris.

That’s a big goal for a company that, when the July 2025 NASA call came, was just Harroun, co-founder and CTO Ari Martinez and a summer intern working out of a one-room office.

If Iris succeeds, Juno’s engines could let satellites run on non-toxic propellants and maneuver far more freely in orbit, something both commercial and defense customers increasingly want. For Harroun, who earned her Ph.D. studying these engines, it would be the payoff of years of work.

Harroun sees the technology as a long-overdue leap. The basic physics behind today’s rocket engines dates to the 1930s and has been refined about as far as it can go, she said, calling it a constraint that’s “been a glass ceiling for too long, in my opinion.”

Harroun grew up south of Seattle in Federal Way. She didn’t come from an aerospace family or spend her childhood dreaming about space. Her dad was a physician and her mom a flight attendant and flight instructor.

What she did pick up at home was an entrepreneurial streak. Her dad ran his own practice for about 20 years, and her mom is now a real estate agent. Harroun said watching them make “something out of completely nothing” has shaped her own path, especially in building Juno.

She calls herself a “late bloomer” who fell for engineering as she was finishing high school and heading to the University of Washington. Sci-fi became an inspiration along the way, and it’s now one of her favorite genres.

She spent all four years at UW working with professor Carl Knowlen, who leads the Aeronautics & Astronautics Department’s Detonation Engines Lab, and she joined the student rocketry team, eventually leading its propulsion group.

Knowlen “sees the potential in everyone,” Harroun said, and the two built a strong relationship that’s still going. Juno’s $1.2 million National Science Foundation grant, awarded this summer, is a partnership with his research group.

Knowlen was also the faculty adviser for the student rocketry team, where he spent “many hot, and sometimes rainy, days” with Harroun and her teammates, test-firing motors and launching high-powered rockets.

“She always was level-headed and led by example,” Knowlen said. “No one worked harder than her to see these tests and launches go off as planned.”

He called her “an exceptional student, natural leader, creative thinker, and very independent,” and said it’s been a great satisfaction to see the engineer she has become.

During college, Harroun interned at NASA, Boeing and Blue Origin. That first stint at Blue Origin, in 2016, set her next move.

“I realized that everyone who had the job that I wanted had gone to Purdue,” she said.

She spent the next six years at Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind., earning a master’s degree and a Ph.D. Her doctoral research was on the technology Juno is now building. She also met Martinez there. The two shared an office for years.

Harroun never planned to stay in academia.

“That just didn’t feel like my calling,” she said. “I wanted to use that very unique experience to get the technical chops to do the type of engineering that I wanted to do.”

Her doctoral advisor, Purdue professor Stephen Heister, still advises her and the company.

“He was one of the people who really pushed me to think about starting this company,” Harroun said. “I think he saw the potential that I had as a founder, both from a technical and a leadership perspective.”

Heister recalled their first technical discussion, when Harroun arrived as a new master’s student. He went deep on nozzle flows, her thesis topic, and the complications of building a nozzle for a detonation engine.

“At the end of my diatribe, she sat quietly and said, ‘You’ve given me a lot to think about,’” Heister said. “I can’t think of any other 22-year-old student with such a response but I knew she was indeed a special talent.”

He described Harroun as having “the unique ability to think deeply and at length,” and said it’s “terribly gratifying” to watch her commercialize the technology she worked on as a grad student.

After finishing her Ph.D. in 2023, Harroun came back to the Seattle region and started Juno. She knew the territory: her UW lab work and the rocketry team had put her in touch with local industry, and Juno now works with some of the same companies she did as a student.

Interning at Blue Origin was the first time she could say “there’s literally a rocket company in our backyard,” Harroun said. Its presence helped build a regional talent pool, which she described as “a contingent of rocket scientists that just live here.”

Starting a company comes with many unknowns, and coming home crossed one off the list.

“I knew how to go start doing stuff immediately,” she said. “So it made that calculus really easy.”

Harroun’s ambitions reach well beyond one demo flight.

“Our mission is to be the rocket engine provider for the U.S.,” she said. “Think of a Rocketdyne.”

That company built engines for the Saturn V and the space shuttle, and it’s now part of L3Harris. Juno wants to play a similar role with a new technology. It’s starting with in-space propulsion for satellites and plans to expand into engines for upper stages, orbital transfer vehicles and, eventually, the boosters that lift rockets off the pad.

The first step is Project Iris. NASA paid Juno about $500,000 through its TechLeap program to build the payload, and it’s also covering the Momentus spacecraft and the flight. There’s no paying customer yet, but the mission is designed to mimic the maneuvers a real satellite would make.

Japan’s space agency has flown rotating detonation engines on suborbital research rockets, but going to orbit is “a whole ‘nother game,” Harroun said. “Going to space is hard. I can attest to that.”

Building a company has taught Harroun things her Ph.D. didn’t. Handling toxic propellants is so complicated, she learned, that operators can spend more fueling a satellite than on “the propulsion system itself, which is kind of crazy.”

The bigger draw is mobility. For decades, satellites have mostly stayed in the orbit a rocket left them in, she said, and “that’s not really acceptable anymore in today’s world.”

To get there, Juno has raised a $1.4 million pre-seed round led by SOSV, on top of its NASA and NSF awards.

As for going to space herself, Harroun admits it would be hard to say no if she got the opportunity.

But the avid hiker and backpacker is partial to terra firma. Her best-case future is one where Earth is the place humanity gets to enjoy and space is what makes that possible.

“I don’t know that I would be the traveler,” Harroun said, “but I’d definitely like to be the enabler.”

#5338. XRP Price Prediction: Bears Are Paying to Short XRP, A Short Squeeze?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP is struggling to reclaim $1, but its derivatives market is showing an increasingly unusual setup. Traders betting against the token are now paying funding fees to maintain their positions. This creates an interesting possibility for the XRP price prediction. If buying pressure returns, bearish traders could face mounting losses and forced liquidations.

However, the market is not quite ready for a bullish victory lap. Open interest is falling, long positions have already suffered heavy liquidations, and XRP still needs to reclaim important resistance levels.

XRP traded around $0.95, following another difficult session for the crypto market. Meanwhile, its futures market is flashing a rate that dropped in aggregated funding to -0.0068% every eight hours, equivalent to roughly -7.4% annually.

Negative funding means short sellers pay long traders to maintain their perpetual futures positions. In other words, bears are effectively paying a premium to maintain their bearish exposure.

Hyperliquid showed an even more pronounced imbalance, with XRP funding reaching approximately -10.2% annually. The figures suggest bearish positioning has become increasingly expensive across several derivatives markets.

However, there is another side to this trade. XRP open interest declined 5.74% over 24 hours to approximately $1.97 billion, so traders are reducing leverage rather than aggressively opening fresh positions.

While XRP traders debate whether another recovery is coming, Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is approaching an important milestone of its own. The Bitcoin Layer 2 project has raised more than $33.2 million during its presale, with its token currently priced at just $0.0136.

The presale is scheduled to conclude on November 26, leaving a narrowing window before its anticipated token launch. Buyers choosing the staking option are also being offered an advertised 35% APY during the presale period.

Bitcoin Hyper aims to bring faster Bitcoin transactions and decentralized applications to a new Layer 2 environment. Its architecture combines Solana Virtual Machine execution with zero-knowledge proofs and Bitcoin settlement.

The project has already introduced testnet components, including its explorer, wallet, faucet, and bridge. With the presale approaching its scheduled conclusion, the remaining allocation and upcoming launch milestone could attract additional attention from traders looking beyond established crypto networks.

The immediate question is whether bearish positioning has become sufficiently expensive to trigger an unexpected reversal. A negative funding rate alone cannot confirm a short squeeze. XRP needs to attract fresh spot buyers, recover momentum, and force short sellers to close their positions.

The first important hurdle remains $1.00. Reclaiming this psychological level could encourage sidelined buyers to return and create additional pressure on leveraged shorts.

A sustained move above $1.00 would put $1.10 within reach, followed by a potential test of $1.20 if short liquidations accelerate.

However, the bearish scenario remains firmly in play. Losing the recent $0.89 low could expose XRP to another decline toward $0.80, particularly if Bitcoin continues weakening.

For now, the XRP price prediction hinges on whether negative funding translates into actual buying pressure. Bears are paying longs, but bulls still need to deliver the rally. If they do, the same traders betting against XRP could become the fuel behind its next recovery.

#5337. Prediction market giant Kalshi is hiring someone to play GTA VI—no resume or cover letter is required, and it pays up to $135,000

Ahead of Grand Theft Auto VI’s release on Thursday, companies across the country could face millions of dollars in lost productivity. But Kalshi is turning that workplace distraction into a high-paying new job. The $40 billion prediction market giant is hiring a “GTA VI Researcher” to play through the entirety of the highly anticipated game.

“We’re looking for someone whose parents said video games would never pay the bills. They were wrong, and you can tell them we said so,” the job listing stated.

The gig comes with a hefty paycheck: a $100,00 to $120,000 fixed project fee, plus an additional $15,000 completion bonus. The successful applicant will begin playing at midnight on November 19—livestreaming with camera via YouTube or Twitch—and continue until beating the game’s story mode.

Exactly how long that will take will vary by player. Rob Nelson, who oversaw the game’s development at Rockstar Games, told The New York Times that his own playthrough in Leonida—the game’s fictional U.S. state name—took about 80 hours, including the main story and some optional side quests.

“I hope that there will be people that want to get up, have a cup of coffee, shower, get dressed, go out for a little exercise,” Nelson said.

Kalshi has explicitly noted that “sleep and touching grass are both allowed,” meaning the researcher won’t have to power through the game in one sitting. But playing through the story is only part of the assignment.

If the Kalshi gig sounds too good to be true, the company has specifically said it’s a “real job.”

Ryan Conlon, who leads talent at Kalshi, said in a LinkedIn post over the weekend that the listing attracted 25,515 applications in less than 48 hours, making it the most-applied-to job in the company’s history.

Not just any gamer will qualify. Kalshi is looking for someone at least 18 years old with a decade of “sweaty” gaming experience, including at least three years of livestreaming. Applicants must also have their own equipment, internet connection, and streaming software. When applying, no resume or cover letter is necessary—instead, just a few multiple-choice and short-answer questions, including, “What’s the first thing you’re doing in Leonida?”

The researcher will also be expected to investigate the in-game economy, produce weekly research reports, and analyze the real-world fallout of the game’s release. They’ll also be tasked with “min-maxing everything”—meaning finding the most efficient strategies and exploiting every possible advantage.

“Find what’s broken, what’s mid, and what’s actually goated, and bring receipts,” the listing added.

Fortune reached out to Kalshi for further comment.

GTA VI is expected to generate billions of dollars in revenue for parent company Take-Two Interactive. But for employers around the world, the game’s release could come with a very different price tag: lost productivity as millions of workers take the day off, call out sick, or sneak away during work hours to play.

But some companies are getting ahead of the inevitable distraction—and even embracing it.

The U.S. Army, for example, used the game’s hype as a recruiting tool, offering active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play the game as an incentive to reenlist.

Meanwhile, $13 billion tech giant Logitech announced last week that it would give its 7,000 global employees a day off to play video games. CEO Hanneke Faber said the dedicated gaming time is expected to actually be a company productivity boost—and she plans to take advantage of the perk herself and spend part of the release day playing GTA VI.

“It’s time to retire the stereotype that gaming is a waste of time,” Faber said at the time. “As a company designing products for work and play, we see every day how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other. ”

Preston Fore is a reporter on Fortune's Success team.

#5336. How hidden text in emails and web pages can hijack a company AI assistant

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Prompt injection attacks let hidden instructions in emails, web pages and files hijack company AI assistants — here is how they work and how to contain them

A company that gives an AI assistant access to its inboxes, shared drives and internal systems is also giving that assistant a way to be steered by strangers. The assistant reads whatever lands in front of it. It cannot reliably tell an instruction from its owner apart from a sentence an outsider planted in an email, a web page or a file.

That weakness has a name: prompt injection. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project, the nonprofit known as OWASP, places it first in its Top 10 for LLM Applications. It holds the LLM01 spot in both the 2023 and 2025 editions of that list.

The danger grows as AI tools move from answering questions to taking actions. A chatbot that gives a wrong answer creates a correction problem. An assistant that can read private files, send messages and call company software creates a security problem. The same model that drafts a reply can be told, by text it was only meant to summarize, to do something its user never asked for.

This guide to prompt injection attacks walks through 10 attack methods and core concepts, a selection rather than a ranked or complete list. It starts with what the attack is and how malicious instructions reach a model, whether typed straight into a chat or hidden inside content the AI reads. It then looks at what attackers try to take, from confidential instructions to private data sent to outside servers. It also explains why AI agents connected to tools and third-party services raise the stakes, and how the attack differs from jailbreaking.

The final slide turns to defense, and the answer there is a partial one. No one has yet found a complete fix. Language models handle trusted instructions and untrusted text together, and no design yet keeps them apart with full reliability. The practical goal for any company deploying these tools is to limit what a hijacked assistant can reach, change or send. Every AI tool with access to company data should be treated as a system that outside text can influence.

Prompt injection is an attack in which text written by an outsider ends up in a language model's input. The model then follows that text as if it were a legitimate instruction from the people who built the tool.

Developer Simon Willison coined the term in September 2022. He modeled the name on SQL injection, a long-known class of web attack. In SQL injection, an attacker types database commands into a field meant for ordinary data, such as a login box or a search bar. A poorly built application then runs those commands against its own database.

The parallel is direct. An AI application starts with instructions from the company that built it. It then adds text from somewhere else — a customer's message, a web page or a document. If that outside text contains an instruction, the model may carry it out in place of the one its developer wrote.

One of the earliest public examples involved a Twitter $TWTR bot run by remoteli.io, a remote-work job site. The bot ran on OpenAI's GPT-3 model and was set up to reply to tweets about remote work. In September 2022, users found they could take it over with plain English. They told the bot to ignore its original instructions and do something else. It complied.

Many of the hijacked replies were jokes. The bot posted whatever strangers on Twitter told it to post, under the company's name.

The episode exposed more than one misbehaving social media account. The attack needed no code, no stolen password and no technical skill. It traveled through the same channel the bot used for normal conversation. Any user who could send the bot a message could also send it new orders.

That feature sets prompt injection apart from many older software flaws. The weak point is not a single faulty line of code that a patch can close. It lies in how language models handle the text they receive. A model that reads outside text can be handed new instructions inside it, whatever job its developer assigned.

Prompt injection comes in two forms. A direct injection is typed into the chat window by the person using the AI tool. An indirect injection hides inside content the AI reads on the user's behalf, such as a web page, an email or a file.

Direct injection is the simpler case. The attacker and the user are the same person. Someone types a message designed to override the instructions a developer gave the model. One example is telling a customer service chatbot to ignore its rules. The attacker needs access to the chat interface, and the hostile text arrives through that person's own session.

Indirect injection changes who the attacker is. The person chatting with the assistant is the victim, not the source of the hostile text. A third party plants instructions in material the assistant will later process. A user might ask the tool to summarize a document, read a message or look something up online. The planted text then enters the model's input alongside the legitimate request.

Kai Greshake and co-authors formalized this second category in a research paper titled "Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection." It was published in February 2023. The title names the core problem. Applications that connect a language model to outside data can be turned against the people who use them.

For companies, indirect injection is the larger concern. The attacker never has to touch the victim's chat. They do not need to log into a company system or persuade an employee to type anything. They only need to put text somewhere the AI tool will eventually read.

This widens the attack surface. With direct injection, the exposure is limited to whoever can reach the chat box. With indirect injection, every source an assistant pulls from becomes a possible entry point. That includes inbound email, shared documents, search results and third-party websites.

The two forms also aim at different targets. A direct attack generally targets the application's own rules. An indirect attack targets the employee relying on the tool, who may never see the instruction that redirected it.

A large language model receives its developer's rules and any outside text as a single stream of tokens in its context window. Nothing in that stream marks one part as a command and another as material to read. The model sees no hard boundary between the two.

Tokens are the small chunks of text — whole words or pieces of words — that a model processes. A workplace AI assistant assembles several kinds of text into that one sequence. The developer's system prompt sits next to the user's question. Retrieved emails, documents or web pages join the same sequence when the assistant needs them.

The model then generates a response from everything it has been given. Position and formatting can hint at where each piece of text came from. Those hints are patterns the model learned in training, not rules it is forced to obey. A line in a retrieved email that reads like a command can shape the answer, even though a stranger wrote it.

SQL injection, an older attack on databases, shows what a structural fix looks like. In that attack, a malicious string typed into a web form gets run as part of a database command. The software industry largely fixed it with parameterized queries. That technique sends the command and the user's input to the database separately. The database treats the input strictly as a value and never executes it as code.

No equivalent complete fix exists for language models. Their usefulness comes from reading natural language and acting on what it says. Instructions and data are written in the same human language. A strict separation at the input level is not available the way it is for a database query.

In 2024, OpenAI researchers published a training method called the instruction hierarchy. It teaches models to favor higher-priority instructions, such as a developer's system message, over lower-priority text like tool outputs. The method reduces the problem. It does not remove it, because the ranking is still learned behavior rather than an enforced barrier.

For companies, the practical result is that any text an AI tool reads is a possible source of instructions. A model asked to summarize a document may also treat that document as a set of orders.

Attackers can plant instructions where a person won't notice them but an AI model will still read them. Common hiding places include white text on a white background, very small fonts and HTML comments.

The trick works because people and language models do not see the same thing. A reader looks at the rendered page or document. A model typically receives the text pulled from the underlying file. That text does not carry the visual cues that tell a person what is meant to be seen.

White text on a white background is the simplest example. The words sit in the document like any other sentence. Their color matches the page. The human eye passes over them. Text set in a tiny font works the same way. It may look like a stray line or a blank gap to a reader, while a model takes in every word.

HTML comments add another layer. They are notes written into a web page's code that browsers do not display at all. A visitor scrolling the page never sees them. An AI tool that processes the page's source can still pick up whatever instructions they contain.

This is a form of indirect prompt injection, in which the attacker never types into the victim's chat. The attacker places text in content the assistant will read later on the user's behalf. That content might be a public web page, an email sent to an employee or a file shared with a team.

The exposure follows the everyday tasks companies hand to AI assistants. An assistant asked to summarize a web page reads the hidden text along with the visible article. One that triages an inbox reads every incoming message, including those from strangers. A research tool that gathers material from many sites reads whatever each of those sites contains.

In each case, the employee sees a clean page or a routine email. The assistant sees the same content plus the concealed instructions.

That gap also makes the attack hard to spot after the fact. An employee reviewing the original email or page will find nothing unusual on the screen. The instruction that changed the assistant's behavior only shows up when someone inspects the raw text or the code behind it.

For a business, the practical implication is that checking a file by eye does not show what an AI tool will read in it. A document can look harmless and still carry text written for the machine rather than the person.

Prompt injection can turn an AI chat window into a channel for stealing data. An injected instruction tells the model to build an image or link whose web address carries private information. When the interface displays it, that information travels to a server the attacker controls.

Markdown is a lightweight formatting language that many chat interfaces use to display text, links and pictures. In markdown, an image is written as a short line of text that points to a web address. When the chat interface renders that line, the user's browser or app requests the image from that address automatically.

The attack exploits that automatic request. A planted instruction asks the model to collect something private from the conversation or the files it can read. The model then adds that material to the end of an image URL as a query string. A query string is the part of a web address that follows a question mark. The attacker's server receives the request and records the full address, private data included. The image itself can be invisible or broken. The user may see nothing unusual.

Links work in a similar way, with one difference. A link sends data only when someone clicks it. The attacker must therefore also persuade the user to click. An image fetch needs no click at all.

Security researcher Johann Rehberger demonstrated variants of this technique against several AI chat products. His demonstrations showed that the pattern was not tied to a single vendor. It followed from a common combination: a model that outside text can steer, and an interface that renders whatever the model writes.

A 2025 case known as EchoLeak brought the pattern into a workplace product. Tracked as CVE-2025-32711, the flaw affected Microsoft $MSFT 365 Copilot, the AI assistant built into Microsoft's workplace apps. Researchers at Aim Security reported it. Microsoft fixed the flaw on the server side, within its own systems.

EchoLeak was described as a zero-click flaw. The victim did not need to open or click anything for the attack to work. That removes a safeguard companies usually rely on: an employee choosing not to open a suspicious message or click a suspicious link.

A system prompt is the hidden set of instructions a company gives its AI model, and users can sometimes extract it with prompt injection. Any business deploying a chatbot should assume the public can read its system prompt and keep secrets out of it.

A widely reported early example came in February 2023. Kevin Liu, a Stanford student, used a prompt injection to get Microsoft $MSFT's Bing Chat to disclose the initial instructions it had been given before any conversation started. Those instructions included an internal codename for the assistant: Sydney.

The leak did not require stolen passwords, insider access or specialist tools. Liu worked through the same chat interface that other Bing Chat users had. The only input was text. The model's own willingness to repeat what it had been told did the rest.

That detail makes system prompt leaks relevant to every company building on a language model. A system prompt sits in front of each conversation and shapes the assistant's behavior. It typically sets a persona and a tone of voice. It can list topics the assistant should avoid, describe products and policies, and explain how to use any connected tools.

Much of that material is harmless if exposed. A competitor that learns a support bot is told to stay polite gains little. The risk comes from what developers sometimes add for convenience. Credentials, API keys, internal URLs, pricing logic, unreleased product details and confidential business rules can all end up written into prompts.

Once such material sits in the prompt, it is only as private as the model's reluctance to repeat it. The Sydney episode showed how thin that protection is. Even an instruction to keep the prompt confidential is just more text the model has read. A well-phrased request can coax the rest back out.

The practical lesson is a design rule rather than a filter. Secrets belong in the systems around the model, such as server-side code and access controls, where the model never sees them. A system prompt should be written on the assumption that it will eventually be published. If a leaked prompt would embarrass the company or hand an attacker a working key, that content needs to move somewhere the model cannot reach.

An AI agent is most exposed to prompt injection when it has three capabilities at once: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally. Developer Simon Willison called this combination the "lethal trifecta" in June 2025.

When all three sit inside one agent, a single injected instruction can direct it to read sensitive information and send that information to an attacker.

Willison also coined the term prompt injection in September 2022. The trifecta is a test of what an agent can do, not of what its prompt says. Each ingredient on its own is an ordinary feature of a workplace assistant. The risk comes from the combination.

Private data covers anything the agent can reach that an outsider should not see. That includes an employee's inbox, shared drives, calendar, source code or customer records.

Untrusted content is any text the agent reads that someone outside the company could have written. An incoming email, a web page, a vendor's shared document or a customer support ticket all qualify. Any of them can carry an instruction aimed at the model.

External communication is any route for information to leave the company. Sending an email, calling a web address, posting to an outside service or producing a clickable link can each serve that purpose.

Take a hypothetical inbox assistant. An attacker emails an employee with an instruction telling the assistant to find recent contracts and forward them to an outside address. The assistant reads the message while processing the inbox, searches the mailbox and sends the files. The employee never has to open the attacker's email.

Tool access is what turns a misleading reply into a real action. An injected instruction runs with whatever permissions the agent holds on the employee's behalf. If the agent can send email, the attacker effectively can too. The same applies to updating a customer record, filing a ticket or approving a calendar invite.

Code execution widens the reach further. An agent that can run commands could be directed to touch files or systems well beyond the task it was given.

The trifecta also gives companies a plain audit question for any agent they deploy. What private data can it read? What outside content reaches it? How can it send information out? An agent with an answer to all three matches Willison's description. Removing any one of the three closes this particular route for data theft.

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an open standard that connects AI assistants to external tools and data. Invariant Labs showed in April 2025 that malicious instructions hidden in an MCP tool's description can steer the agent that uses it.

Anthropic introduced MCP in November 2024. Each connection runs through an MCP server, which offers the assistant a set of tools along with a written description of each one.

A tool description is the short block of text that tells a model what a tool does and when to call it. The model reads that text as part of its working context. A person installing the tool may see only its name or a brief summary in an app's interface. That gap gives an attacker room to work.

In a tool poisoning attack, whoever writes or controls a tool slips extra instructions into its description. The text might tell the assistant to read a file it was never asked to open. It might tell the assistant to pass information along to a different tool. The model treats the description as guidance on how to behave. It can then follow those planted instructions even though the user asked for nothing unusual.

In May 2025, Invariant Labs reported a related attack on an agent using the GitHub MCP server. The setup was a malicious issue posted in a public repository. An agent connected to a user's account could read that issue. The planted text could then lead it to leak data from the user's private repositories.

The GitHub case relied on content the agent read, not on a doctored tool. The attack text arrived through a trusted, official connector.

This makes MCP a supply-chain problem as much as a model problem. Each MCP server a company connects is a piece of third-party software that speaks directly to its AI assistant. Its descriptions, and the data it returns, become text the model may act on.

One slide-specific step for security teams is to review each MCP server like any other software dependency. That review covers who publishes it, what its tool descriptions say and which accounts and data it can reach.

Jailbreaking tries to get a language model to break its own safety training, for example by producing content it would normally refuse. Prompt injection targets something else: an application that mixes a developer's trusted instructions with untrusted text from outside.

Developer Simon Willison, who coined the term prompt injection in September 2022, has drawn this distinction. The two attacks can look alike on the screen. They describe different problems.

In a typical jailbreak, the person typing is the one trying to misuse the model. The target is the set of guardrails the model's maker built in during training. A successful jailbreak produces an answer the model was trained to withhold. The person who asked for that answer is the one who receives it.

Prompt injection works differently. The attacker is often not the person using the tool. The attacker's words arrive inside text the application handles, and the model treats them as commands. The target is the application and the person relying on it, not the model's content rules.

The techniques overlap. Both rely on phrasing that persuades a model to set aside the instructions it was given. A message telling a model to ignore its earlier rules could appear in either kind of attack. The difference lies in who is being attacked and whose instructions get overridden.

That difference shapes who handles the risk inside a company. Resistance to jailbreaks sits largely with the model provider, which controls the safety training. Exposure to prompt injection depends on how a company builds and connects its own AI tools. That includes what data an assistant can see, what outside content it reads and what actions it can take.

A model that refuses every harmful request can still follow an injected instruction to forward an email or send a confidential file's contents to an outsider. Neither action breaks a safety rule. Each one breaks the application's intended behavior.

For security teams, the working test is short. A jailbreak changes what a model will say. A prompt injection changes whom the model works for.

Prompt injection has no complete fix today. The practical defense is containment: restrict what a hijacked AI tool can touch and do, so a successful attack does limited harm.

That changes the question security teams ask. They stop asking whether an assistant can be tricked. They assume it can be, and they plan for the moment it is. The controls that follow are familiar security practices applied to a new kind of software.

Least-privilege access is the starting point. An AI tool should hold only the permissions its job requires. A meeting summarizer does not need to send email. A coding assistant does not need access to payroll records. Every permission an assistant lacks is one an injected instruction cannot use.

Human approval adds a checkpoint before actions that are hard to undo. Sending an email, moving money, deleting files or changing account settings can each be held until a person confirms them. This step adds friction. It also means a hidden instruction cannot complete a sensitive task on its own.

Limiting outbound channels narrows the ways data can leave. An agent that can contact only an approved list of addresses or domains has fewer routes to an attacker's server. Blocking arbitrary web requests and unapproved links in an assistant's output closes off common exit points.

Logging tool calls gives security teams a record of what an assistant did and when. If an injection succeeds, those logs show which data was read and where it was sent. They also help teams spot unusual behavior sooner.

Red-teaming tests these controls before attackers do. Teams plant injection attempts in the documents, emails and web pages an assistant will process, then check whether it follows them. The tests need repeating after each model or tool change. A new version can respond differently to the same attack.

Input and output filters scan text for suspicious instructions and can catch known attack patterns. They do not offer complete protection. An attacker can reword an instruction in many ways, and a filter can flag only what it recognizes.

Longer-term fixes remain at the research stage. Google $GOOGL DeepMind published a design called CaMeL in 2025 that separates trusted instructions from untrusted data at the system level. The approach does not depend on the model to tell the two apart. CaMeL is a research proposal, not a deployed fix. Until an approach like it is proven in production, containment remains the main line of defense for companies running AI tools.

#5335. Araceli raises $4.5M for drug discovery tools aimed at reducing animal testing

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 4:38 pm

Araceli Biosciences, a Portland-area biotech company, has secured $4.5 million in funding to help commercialize technology and develop new products that support using human cells instead of animal studies to test new drugs.

The Tigard, Ore., startup offers instruments and software for creating images of cells and automating analysis. Its technologies fall under the umbrella term “New Approach Methodologies,” which includes human-tissue models, computer simulations and AI-based approaches that reduce or avoid experimentation on animals such as mice, rats and monkeys.

Supporters of the methods, known as NAMs, argue that they can yield better outcomes because animals are not a perfect substitute for humans and can generate irrelevant findings. That can lead to costly, time-intensive development of drugs that fail to perform in people. Advocates also promote the alternatives as more humane.

The National Institutes of Health announced $84 million in September to build infrastructure for NAMs research at 10 sites nationwide.

“[T]he efforts signal a significant investment into human-based technologies as the future of preclinical science, aiming to make research faster, more predictive, and more directly relevant to human health,” the NIH said in a release.

Araceli said it has raised a total of $22.7 million from investors. The new round was led by William Cortelyou and included Fluke Venture Partners, according to PitchBook. The company disclosed Thursday that businessman and animal welfare advocate Jeff Swickard was also an investor.

Swickard owns 54 auto dealerships across Western states and is a commercial real estate investor with $250 million invested in Portland properties.

Shawn MacDonald, chief financial officer for Araceli, said Swickard’s “support reflects a belief that we share, which is that better science and more humane science go hand-in-hand.”

Araceli launched in 2023 as a spinoff from Phoseon Technology, which makes UV LED units for industrial curing and life sciences applications.

The company said that companies and institutions using Araceli technology include the Max Planck Institute and Evotec in Germany, the Wertheim UF Scripps Institute in Florida, VALID Therapeutics in Boston, and Ginkgo Bioworks, as well as large pharmaceutical companies. It has 30 employees.

#5333. Optum’s CEO still works weekends as a pediatrician. What he sees ‘should not happen in America, but it does every single day’

On his last couple of weekends working as a hospital pediatrician in Boston, Dr. Patrick Conway saw three patients he can’t stop talking about.

One was a 14-year-old girl who had called more than 100 people trying to get mental health care before she ended up in his hospital with broken legs. Another was a 21-year-old with meningitis. “She wakes up. What’s the first thing she says? I’m a single mother. I can’t afford this. I got to get out of here,” Conway said. The third was a 15-year-old on Medicaid who needed complex rehab for a neurologic disorder, and the hospital was struggling to find anywhere to send her.

“That should not happen in America, but it does every single day,” he said.

During the week, Conway runs Optum, the health services arm of UnitedHealth Group, which he said employs about 300,000 of the conglomerate’s roughly 400,000 people. That makes him one of the more unusual witnesses to American health care’s failures, because his company sits on the other side of many of them. Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, he told Fortune’s Diane Brady that the weekend shifts are the point. “Those stories could be anywhere in America,” he said, and Optum’s job is “to prevent those stories from occurring in the future.”

Brady put the tension more bluntly. Optum, she said, is a bit like the cable guy: people need it, and they don’t always love it. Conway didn’t argue with that. He said Optum’s business customers (health systems, payers, employers) are “generally quite positive.” On the insurance side, “people have concerns,” he said, listing access, prior authorization and whether their doctors are in network.

Conway took over Optum in 2025, a year in which UnitedHealth replaced CEO Andrew Witty with former CEO, Stephen Hemsley, and said it was cooperating with federal investigations into its Medicare business.

Conway has seen the system from most of its angles. He joined Health and Human Services as chief medical officer late in the George W. Bush administration and held several roles at Medicare and Medicaid, mostly under Barack Obama, “which is a little less common these days.” He has also run a Blues plan. His first week as an attending physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, he said, a child arrived with a 1,000-page paper chart after years of bouncing between community hospitals. On page 487, he spotted a rare mitochondrial disorder. “In today’s world, that child should be diagnosed anywhere in America … within seconds, minutes,” he said.

His case for Optum is that scale and AI can close those gaps faster than a fragmented system can. On affordability, he pointed to Optum Rx’s Savings IQ tool. He said it brought the median copay for specialty drugs down from about $88 to $5 and saved consumers more than $1 billion out of pocket over the past 12 months. One patient with cancer emailed him to say he’d been going on and off his medicine because it cost about $300, and he hadn’t told his wife. “Now it’s $5,” Conway said. “I’m on my medicine. I’m doing better.”

He also pitched OptumReal, which digitizes benefits and connects payers with health systems. Conway said it can approve a service with “99 plus percent accuracy,” so the payer, the provider and the patient all see the same number at the point of care. “That’s how healthcare should work,” he said. Asked when it would be the norm, he said it “may become faster than you imagine,” because payers and providers “know the system doesn’t work as it is today.”

Brady also asked about Mark Cuban, who has spent years arguing that pharmacy benefit managers like Optum Rx are what’s driving drug prices up. Conway noted he once debated Cuban in Washington: “I think he was a little surprised. I accepted the debate.” He called Cuban’s model “a niche solution for some number of drugs” that helps people, and said the system needs something more comprehensive.

Brady raised Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla’s argument that cancer will one day be as manageable as diabetes. Conway, who lost his father to cancer, said he hopes Bourla is right. “It may take a little longer,” he said.

He closed on time. He’s been trying to fix health care for 20 to 25 years, he said. “I don’t know if I’ve got another 20. I hope so. It’s got to go faster.”

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.
