#5332. Blue Origin puts its space station plans on hold to concentrate on moon missions instead

by Alan Boyle on Nov 13, 2026 at 2:35 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 2:35 pm

Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture has decided not to seek further NASA funding for its Orbital Reef space station project in order to tighten its focus on lunar missions.

For the past five years, Blue Origin has played a lead role in Orbital Reef, alongside partners including Sierra Space and Boeing. In late 2021, Blue Origin won a $130 million contract from NASA in the first phase of the space agency’s Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program, or CLD.

Now NASA is seeking proposals for the next phase of the program, which will fund the development of orbital outposts to replace International Space Station in the 2030s. Proposals are due on Dec. 8, with contracts expected to be awarded next spring.

Blue Origin indicated that it will not submit a bid.

“Blue Origin’s mission is to build a road to space for the benefit of Earth so that millions of people can live and work in space. Establishing a sustained human presence on the moon is a critical step toward that future,” the company said in an emailed statement.

“As our role supporting NASA’s Artemis and Moon Base missions continues to grow, we’re focusing resources on capabilities that directly advance our lunar projects,” Blue Origin said. “By sharpening that focus, we can move faster on the technologies and infrastructure needed to make lunar permanence a reality.”

Orbital Reef was once touted as a “mixed-use business park” in space — and was even slated to star in a sci-fi thriller titled “Helios.” But much like that delayed film project, the space station is now on the back burner.

Orbital Reef isn’t the only initiative Blue Origin has put on hold to prioritize moon missions. In January, the company suspended its suborbital New Shepard program for at least two years for similar reasons.

Blue Origin is building landers for delivering cargo and crews to the lunar surface for NASA. An uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1 lunar lander is scheduled for launch early next year, and a crew-capable Mark 2 version is scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA’s Artemis 3 mission.

Last week, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, plus a $140 million option, to deliver a nuclear-powered rover to the lunar south pole. Blue Origin also won a spot in NASA’s broader lunar cargo delivery program. In addition, Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, will contribute to a lunar power-generating project known as miniCAST.

Blue Origin is pursuing several other moon development initiatives, including a program called Blue Alchemist that aims to use lunar materials to manufacture solar cells and electrical wire.

Several competitors are still working on commercial space stations. Voyager Technologies, Airbus and Northrop Grumman lead the Starlab consortium, which received CLD Phase 1 funding from NASA and is expected to put in a proposal for Phase 2.

Axiom Space and Vast are also developing outposts that could take the place of the ISS. Meanwhile, Marysville, Wash.-based Gravitics is building space station hardware for Axiom and an orbital carrier for the U.S. Space Force.

#5331. Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The company says R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery said the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the company, cost nothing.

The reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as new rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he said, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

The risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

The details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent company, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

The bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

For everyday users, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

The trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

#5330. Silt, rust, wiring and titles: 12 places to look for flood damage in a used car

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Learn how to spot a flood-damaged used car with 12 checks, from musty smells and silt to title brands, before a hidden water problem becomes yours

A car that sat in floodwater can look clean again by the time it reaches a sales lot. The water drains out. The carpets get shampooed or replaced, and the paint gets a wash and a coat of wax. The damage that matters most often stays out of sight. It sits in wiring harnesses, electrical connectors, seat padding and metal parts that corrode slowly from the inside.

That gap between appearance and condition is what makes flood cars a risk for used-car buyers. Water and the corrosion it leaves behind can affect airbags, lights, power accessories and engine components. Some of those problems show up right away. Others take weeks or months to surface, long after the sale is final.

Flooded vehicles tend to reach the used market after major events such as hurricanes, when large numbers of cars are damaged at once. Some are declared total losses and branded with a flood or salvage title. Others are moved to another state, where title rules differ. Some were never claimed on insurance at all. Those cars can carry a clean title even though water reached the cabin or the engine.

Knowing how to spot a flood-damaged used car comes down to looking in the places a quick cleanup tends to miss. The 12 checks in this list range from quick sensory clues to paperwork and a mechanic's inspection. They start with smell and sight inside the cabin. Others cover the electrical system, the title history, the engine bay, the fluids, the seat belts and the undercarriage.

No single check settles the question on its own. Foggy headlights can come from a cracked seal. Milky oil can point to a failed head gasket. Light rust on brake rotors is normal for a car that has been parked for a while. What carries weight is a pattern of several clues pointing the same way. A seller's account that does not match what the car shows is another clue in that pattern.

Each check below can be done on its own. Most need little more than a flashlight, some time and a willingness to lift carpet edges and look under seats. The combined results give a buyer a clearer basis for deciding whether to keep negotiating, pay for a professional inspection or walk away from the deal.

A damp, moldy odor in the cabin is among the most common signs that floodwater got inside a used car. Treat that smell as a cue to inspect the vehicle closely before talking price.

Water that reaches the interior soaks into carpet padding, seat foam and the insulation behind trim panels. Those materials hold moisture long after the surfaces feel dry. Mold and mildew can then grow where no one sees them. The odor is often the first thing that gives them away.

Sellers sometimes try to hide it. A flooded car may arrive with several air fresheners clipped to the vents, or with the heavy scent of shampoo and cleaning products. A strong perfume smell in an otherwise ordinary used car is worth noting on its own. It may be covering something.

Do the smell test with the doors and windows closed. Let the car sit shut for a few minutes first if possible. Odors build up in a closed cabin. A car aired out before the showing can hide a problem that returns once the doors close.

Start the engine and run the heater, then the air conditioning. Put your face near the vents and breathe in. Mold can settle inside the ductwork and around the climate system. A musty blast from the vents points to moisture in places that surface cleaning cannot reach.

Fine silt, sand or dried mud in hidden corners of a car is a strong sign that floodwater got inside. A seller can shampoo the visible carpet, but sediment tends to stay in crevices that routine cleaning misses.

Floodwater rarely stays clear. It picks up soil, sand and organic debris as it moves, and it carries that material into the cabin. When the water drains away, the heavier particles settle and dry in place. What remains is often a thin layer of gray or brown grit that feels powdery between the fingers.

Start under the front seats. Slide each seat fully forward and then fully back, and shine a flashlight into the floor area in both positions. The seat-track channels deserve a close look. These narrow metal grooves trap fine particles that a vacuum nozzle struggles to reach.

Rust on seat rails, seat springs, pedal assemblies or the screws under the dashboard can point to flood damage. These metal parts sit inside the cabin. In a car whose interior has stayed dry, they should show little or no corrosion.

Automakers protect exterior and underbody steel against rain, road spray and winter salt. Much of the hardware inside the cabin gets less protection because it is meant to stay dry. When floodwater fills the interior, those parts can sit in water for hours or days. Corrosion can follow.

Start with the seat rails. These are the metal tracks the seats slide along when a driver adjusts them forward and back. Move each front seat through its full range and look at the tracks with a flashlight. Orange or brown scale, pitting, or a stiff, gritty motion are all worth noting.

Electrical problems are among the clearest signs of flood damage in a used car. Water and the corrosion it leaves behind attack wiring and connectors. Test every powered feature in the cabin, and watch the dashboard for warning lights that flicker or refuse to go out.

Much of a car's wiring runs along the floor beneath the carpet and under the seats. That routing puts it low enough to sit in standing water during a flood. Connectors in those areas can keep corroding after the cabin has been dried and cleaned.

Start with the basics. Raise and lower each power window from the driver's master switch and from its own door switch. Lock and unlock the doors with the interior buttons and the key fob. Move each power seat through its full range in every direction.

Open the hood and look for silt, dried debris, a faint waterline and white or green corrosion on electrical terminals. These marks show that water rose high enough to reach parts the car's body normally shields from rain and road spray.

Start with the low areas at the front of the engine compartment. Floodwater carries leaves, grass, twigs and fine mud, and it drops them where the current slows. Look in the gaps around the radiator and air-conditioning condenser, behind the grille and along the ledges beside the headlight mounts. Crusted mud in crevices that a hose would not easily reach deserves a closer look.

Open the air filter housing as well. On many cars the air intake sits fairly low in the engine bay. A stained, warped or dirt-caked filter is a warning sign. So is silt or a water mark inside the housing. Either one suggests water reached the intake. Water drawn into a running engine cannot be compressed, and it can bend connecting rods. Mechanics call this failure hydrolock.

Pull each seat belt out to its full length and inspect the webbing along its whole run. Water stains, dried mud, stiffness or a gritty texture on the belt are strong signs that floodwater rose into the cabin.

This check works because of where the belt is stored. Most of the webbing stays wound on a spring-loaded spool inside the retractor. On front belts, that retractor usually sits low in the door pillar, close to the floor. When water fills a cabin, it reaches the retractor early.

The part of the belt a buyer normally sees is easy to wipe clean. The section rolled up on the spool is not. A seller can scrub the exposed strap and still miss the stained length hidden inside the housing. On a car that has stayed dry, that stored webbing should look and feel much like the rest of the belt.

An independent pre-purchase inspection is the strongest final check before buying a car you suspect was flooded. If the seller refuses one, or the car's history does not match what you find, walk away.

Choose the mechanic yourself rather than using one the seller recommends. A shop with no stake in the sale has no reason to overlook trouble. Arrange the visit before any money changes hands, and ask for the findings in writing.

A professional inspection reaches places a buyer in a parking lot cannot. A shop can raise the car on a lift, remove trim panels and examine wiring harnesses that sit out of sight. A mechanic can also connect a scan tool to the OBD-II port. That diagnostic port has been standard on cars sold in the U.S. since the 1996 model year. Stored trouble codes can point to faults the dashboard does not display.

Ask whether the cabin air filter, on cars that have one, can be checked. A filter that looks damp, discolored or furry with growth adds weight to the smell.

A musty odor does not prove a flood by itself. A leaking door or windshield seal, a blocked sunroof drain or a clogged air conditioning drain can also leave water in the cabin. Any of those problems still means moisture has been sitting inside the car. The smell justifies a closer look, not a final verdict.

The glove box is the next place to check. It sits well above the floor. Dirt inside it suggests the water rose high in the cabin. Empty it completely and run a finger along the corners and seams. Look at the owner's manual and any papers stored there for wrinkled, warped or water-stained pages.

The trunk comes next. Lift the floor cover and take out the spare tire if possible. The spare-tire well is a low point in the body, and water and mud tend to pool there. Check the jack and tool compartments in the same area for grit or a dried crust.

Finish beneath the dashboard. Get down into the footwell and look up behind the pedals and along the lower edge of the dash. Dried mud or debris clinging to the underside of the dash suggests water reached well above the floor.

Location matters as much as the material. A car used for beach trips can carry sand in the footwells and cargo area. Grit tucked high under the dashboard or inside a closed glove box points more toward flooding. Leaves, grass or small twigs lodged in these same spots add weight to that reading.

A faint horizontal stain running across seat fabric, door panels or the trunk liner can show how high floodwater rose inside a car. Carpet that looks newer than the rest of the cabin, sits loose or does not match can point to a replacement after water damage.

These lines form as floodwater recedes and the fabric dries. Dirt and minerals carried in the water collect at the edge of the wet area and leave a band behind. On light upholstery the mark may show as a brown or gray line. On darker fabric it can be faint. Look at the seats and panels from a low angle in good daylight.

Check whether any line sits at roughly the same height around the cabin. A stain on one seat cushion could come from a spilled drink. A level line that carries across both front seats, the rear bench and the lower door panels is much harder to explain that way.

The trunk needs the same attention. Pull back the trunk liner and any side panels that come loose by hand. Stains or rippled fabric there can show that water sat in the cargo area.

Carpet is commonly replaced on a flooded car. Saturated padding dries slowly and can hold moisture long after the surface feels dry. Carpet that is new, loose or a slightly different color or texture from the surrounding trim suggests it was replaced. So does fresh-looking carpet in an older car whose pedals and seat bolsters show heavy wear.

Lift a corner of the carpet near the door sill, or under a floor mat where it pulls up. The padding beneath should be dry and clean. Damp padding, dark staining or a crusty texture on the backing are warning signs.

Replacement carpet alone does not prove a car was flooded. Owners replace worn or stained carpet for many ordinary reasons. Ask the seller why it was changed, and weigh the answer against the other clues in the cabin.

Look beneath the seats at the springs and the seat frame next. These parts sit low in the cabin. Water rising through the floor reaches them early.

The driver's footwell comes after that. Check the brake and accelerator pedal arms, the brackets that hold them and the pivot points where they mount. Look up under the dashboard at the screws and fasteners that hold trim panels and wiring brackets in place. Rusted screw heads in a spot no rain could reach are hard to explain without water inside the car.

Weigh what you find against the car's age and history. An older car from a snowy region can show some corrosion in places owners rarely look. A late-model car with rusty pedal brackets and an otherwise tidy interior is a mismatch worth questioning.

Saltwater makes the problem worse. Salt generally speeds up corrosion. A car caught in coastal storm surge can show heavier rust than one that sat in freshwater from a river or heavy rain. Ask where the car was registered and driven. A history near the coast around the time of a major storm adds weight to any rust found inside the cabin.

Condensation, standing water or a visible waterline inside a headlight or taillight housing can mean the car sat in deep water. Lamp housings are sealed units. Moisture trapped inside is a clue worth noting, though it is not proof on its own.

Headlights and taillights are built to keep weather out. Each lens is bonded to a housing. Most assemblies also have small vents that let air pressure even out as the bulbs heat and cool. When floodwater rises above the height of the lamps, water can push past those seals and vents and collect inside.

What the water leaves behind is often more telling than the water itself. Look through each lens for a faint horizontal line across the reflector. Look for a ring of dried residue, or for grit and silt settled in the lowest corner of the housing. A line at the same height on lamps at both ends of the car points to standing water. A single leak is less likely to explain it.

Check the lower lamps as well. Fog lights, side marker lights and the lower sections of some taillights sit closer to the ground than the main headlights. Rising water reaches them first. They can show moisture even when the higher lamps look clear.

A light mist on its own is a weaker signal. A cracked lens, a failed seal or a blocked vent can let humid air into an otherwise dry car. Some vented lamps also show a thin film of condensation after rain or a car wash. That kind of condensation usually clears once the lights have been on for a while. Droplets that stay, or water pooling at the bottom of the housing, are harder to explain away.

Compare the left and right lamps. On an older car, one clear lens next to a yellowed partner may mean that lamp was replaced. A full set of new lamps on a car that otherwise shows its age raises the same question. Replacement can also follow a minor collision. Ask the seller why the parts were changed.

Moisture in the lamps carries the most weight when it lines up with other signs of water exposure elsewhere in the car. On its own, it is a reason to look harder, not a verdict.

Then work through the rest of the cabin. Turn on the radio and the infotainment screen. Run the wipers at each speed and try the washer spray. Check the horn, turn signals, hazard lights, power mirrors and any sunroof. Switch on each interior light, then walk around the car to confirm the headlights, brake lights and reverse lights work.

Pay attention to how each feature behaves, not only whether it responds. A window that moves slowly or stalls partway can point to a weak or corroded connection. So can a light that dims or flickers, or a gauge needle that jumps without reason.

The dashboard needs its own check. When the ignition is first switched on, most warning lights illuminate briefly as a self-test. They should go out once the engine starts. A light that stays on, flickers or comes and goes during a drive needs an explanation from the seller.

The airbag warning light needs particular attention. A fault in the airbag system can affect whether the airbags deploy in a crash. An airbag light that never appears during the self-test is also a concern. Someone can remove or disconnect the bulb to hide a fault.

A clean result on the day of a viewing is not the final word. Electrical problems from flooding can surface weeks or months later as corrosion works through connectors and wiring. A car that behaves normally during a short visit can still develop faults after the sale. Repeating the checks at the end of a longer test drive gives intermittent problems more time to show up.

A vehicle history report can show whether a car carries a flood or salvage brand on its title. Run one before any money changes hands, and treat a clean result as one piece of evidence rather than proof.

A title brand is a label a state motor vehicle agency adds to a car's ownership record to flag a past problem. A flood brand points to water damage. A salvage brand usually means an insurer declared the car a total loss. The exact wording, and the conditions that trigger each brand, differ from state to state.

Commercial services such as Carfax and AutoCheck gather title records and other reported events into one vehicle history. The U.S. Department of Justice oversees a separate database, the National Motor Vehicle Title Information System, known as NMVTIS. Consumers reach NMVTIS data through approved private providers. The system is meant to show whether a car has carried a brand in any participating state. Checking more than one of these sources can turn up a record that another one missed.

Every report starts with the vehicle identification number, or VIN. That 17-character code sits on a plate at the base of the windshield on the driver's side. It also appears on a label in the driver's door jamb. Compare both with the VIN printed on the title and on the report. A mismatch is a reason to stop the deal.

A clean report does not prove a car stayed dry. A flooded car taken to another state can sometimes be retitled there without its original brand. This practice is known as title washing. A car whose owner never filed an insurance claim may never have been reported as flooded at all. In either case, the paperwork can look clean while the damage remains.

Read the full report, not just the summary line. Look closely at a recent registration in an area hit by flooding, a fresh title issued in a new state, or several ownership changes in a short span. Ask the seller to explain each one. Then compare the answers with what the car itself shows.

The underhood fuse and relay box comes next. Lift its cover and check the fuse blades, the relay pins and the sockets around them. Green or white crust, a dull grayish film or a dried water ring inside the box are all red flags. The box is built to resist splashes, not submersion.

Check the wiring harness connectors you can reach, along with the battery terminals. Some white or blue-green buildup on battery posts can come from ordinary battery venting. Corrosion spread across many connectors well away from the battery is harder to explain that way.

Bare metal offers another clue. Steel brackets, bolt heads and fasteners under the hood tend to stay fairly clean on a car that has never sat in water. Road salt in snowy regions can also rust them. The pattern matters more than the rust itself. Fresh orange rust across many of these parts, stopping at a similar height, points to prolonged contact with water.

An unusually spotless engine bay on an older car also warrants a question. Thorough detailing can remove the debris and staining described above. Ask the seller when the engine was cleaned and why.

Pull the engine oil dipstick and look for oil that appears milky, frothy or the color of a light-brown milkshake. That look, or water droplets in the transmission fluid, can mean water got inside parts that are supposed to stay sealed.

Healthy engine oil ranges from amber when fresh to dark brown or black as it ages. It should look smooth and consistent on the dipstick. When water mixes with oil, the two churn into an emulsion. The result is a pale, creamy sludge that does not match normal oil at any stage of its life.

The underside of the oil filler cap is a second place to look. Remove the cap on top of the engine and check for a tan or beige residue. A thin film there can also come from condensation in an engine driven only on short trips in cold weather. The residue carries more weight when the dipstick shows the same thing.

Milky oil does not prove a car was flooded. A failed head gasket can let coolant leak into the oil and produce nearly the same appearance. A cracked cylinder head can do it too. Either cause calls for a mechanic's diagnosis before any money changes hands.

Transmission fluid needs its own check. On many automatic transmissions, fresh fluid is red and darkens with use. Water contamination can turn it pink, cloudy or foamy, or leave visible droplets on the dipstick. Many newer cars have sealed transmissions with no dipstick. On those models, a shop may need to pull a fluid sample.

Water inside an engine can cause damage well beyond dirty oil. Water can enter the cylinders through the air intake. Unlike air, water does not compress. A piston rising against trapped water cannot finish its stroke, a failure known as hydrolock. The force can bend connecting rods.

The axle differentials have vents that let air move in and out as they heat and cool. On a submerged car, those vents can let water inside. The gear oil can then turn milky in the same way engine oil does.

Fresh fluid is not proof that a car stayed dry. A seller can change the oil and transmission fluid before listing a vehicle. Very clean fluid in an older, high-mileage car is a reason to ask the seller when it was changed. Service receipts can show when the work was done and why.

Run the strap slowly between your fingers as it comes out. Look for a stain line or a change in color partway along it. Feel for crusty patches where silt dried into the weave. Then let the belt go and watch it retract. A belt that drags, hesitates or stops short may have debris or corrosion in the mechanism. Check the rear belts as well as the front ones, including the center position.

The bolts that fasten the seats to the floor are the second part of this check. Seats are sometimes taken out of a flooded car so the carpet and padding underneath can dry or be replaced. That job leaves traces on the hardware.

Signs of removal include scratched paint on the bolt heads, rounded edges from a wrench and bolts that don't match each other. Fresh tool marks on otherwise aged hardware are worth raising with the seller. Removing a seat also means unplugging its wiring connectors. In many modern cars, those connectors serve power controls, seat heaters or side airbags. Disturbed or loose connectors under a seat add weight to the same suspicion.

A seat taken out for an ordinary repair can show some of these marks too. Ask why it came out, and ask for the repair paperwork. A belt that fails to retract or lock properly is also a safety problem. It needs a mechanic's attention before the car goes back on the road.

Heavy rust, flaking metal or caked-on mud across the frame, suspension, differential and brake lines can point to a car that sat in floodwater. The warning sign is deep corrosion on parts that are usually protected. A thin orange film on brake rotors is a different matter. It forms on bare iron after rain or a humid night, and the first few stops wipe it away.

The underbody sits lowest and stays submerged longest when a car is caught in rising water. Mud and silt settle into its crevices, and moisture can linger long after the cabin has been cleaned. A flashlight and a look from beneath the car make these areas easier to judge. A repair shop's lift gives a clearer view.

Start with the frame rails and crossmembers. Flaking or scaly rust suggests metal that stayed wet for a long time. An even, light film is less telling. Look for mud packed onto the tops of rails and brackets. Road spray tends to coat lower surfaces. Dried mud resting on upper ledges is harder to explain by ordinary driving.

Control arms, coil springs, shock absorbers and their mounting bolts deserve the same scrutiny. Caked mud around spring seats and bushings can indicate a long soak. So can heavy corrosion on bolt heads. Compare the condition of these parts with the car's age and mileage.

On rear-wheel-drive and four-wheel-drive vehicles, check the differential housing for rust and dried residue. A differential has a vent to release pressure, and floodwater can enter through it. A mechanic can drain the fluid and look for water contamination.

Brake lines are thin metal tubes that run along the underbody to each wheel. Swelling, scaling or deep pitting on these lines is a safety concern whatever the cause. A car with that kind of damage needs a mechanic's assessment before purchase.

The exhaust system offers weaker evidence on its own. Pipes, mufflers and heat shields rust with age on many cars. Repeated heating and cooling, along with moisture that condenses inside the pipes, speeds that process. Mud or debris lodged behind heat shields is a more specific clue than rust alone.

Road salt complicates the picture. Cars driven through winters in states that salt their roads often show underbody rust with no flood history. Underbody rust carries the most weight when it appears alongside other signs. Silt in the cabin or a registration history in an area that recently flooded are two examples.

Tell the mechanic up front that flood damage is the concern. That focus shapes where the inspection looks and what the mechanic checks first.

Timing and location add context. A car listed in the months after a hurricane or other major flood warrants extra scrutiny. So does one registered in or near the affected region.

Ask the seller directly whether the car has ever been in water, and note the answer. Then compare that account with the physical evidence and the paperwork. A claim that the car was always garaged inland means little if the inspection turns up corrosion and dried sediment.

Several situations justify ending the talks. One is a seller who will not allow an inspection. Others include pressure to close quickly, a push to pay in cash or reluctance to show the title. Gaps or contradictions in the vehicle's story belong on the same list.

The terms of the sale also shape what happens afterward. In the U.S., dealers must post a Buyers Guide on used cars stating whether the vehicle is sold as is. A car bought as is usually leaves the buyer with little recourse once problems surface.

#5329. Altria CEO says ‘responsibility needs to be at the heart’ of its FDA-regulated nicotine business. It’s part of why it sued the regulator

As Big Tobacco companies pivot away from combustible products to less harmful nicotine alternatives, they’re finding new challenges in their relationships with regulators.

Sal Mancuso, the CEO of Altria Group, which owns cigarette and cigar brands like Marlboro and Black & Mild,  explained at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday that competing in a Food and Drug Administration-regulated industry brings with it both an added sense of responsibility to consumers, and hurdles in competing with other businesses in the space. Mancuso said that Altria’s On! nicotine pouch brand is a key innovation for the company, but regulations have slowed growth.

The Marlboro-maker announced its Moving Beyond Smoking initiative in 2023 as more consumers move away from cigarettes, putting a renewed focus on smoke-free alternatives to cigarettes such as NJOY vapes and On! nicotine pouches, which are competing with Philip Morris’s Zyn.

“You can call us the underdog in the pouch category today, but our intention is to lead the pouch category over the long term,” Mancuso told Fortune Executive Editorial Director Diane Brady. “When you think about what’s maybe getting in the way, there’s a couple of factors: One is just the misperception that nicotine is what causes harm from tobacco use. Most of the harm is from combustion, so clarifying that misperception is important. And then we are regulated by the FDA. When you’re in the nicotine business, responsibility needs to be at the heart of everything you do.”

Altria, through its subsidiaries Helix Innovations and NJOY, sued the FDA in September, claiming the agency blocked newer nicotine products from reaching the market through its review process, which the nicotine company is seeking to overhaul. Through the Premarket Tobacco Product Application (PMTA), the FDA is legally required to review new tobacco products before they reach market and decide if the product provides an overall public health benefit within 180 days of submitting an application. Altria claims the FDA has failed to meet that deadline, and that the regulator’s red tape and bureaucracy stalled newer On! products from reaching the market, while foreign competitors flood store shelves.

The FDA said it would consider revisions to the PMTA and consider new rules as the market continues to change, and last month, U.S. District Judge James Wesley Hendrix of the Northern District of Texas granted a joint request from the FDA and the plaintiffs to pause litigation.

Mancuso explained that Altria sued the FDA because it needed enforcement against illicit products. Reiterating what was in the lawsuit, he said what should take the FDA six months to review was taking six years in some cases, allowing illegal products, particularly from China, from not just taking market share, but also skirting standards Mancuso believes the FDA should keep in place to protect the safety of the consumer. He claimed competing overseas products are marketed in vape shops as made in the U.S.A, but are mislabeled.

“Quite frankly, the regulations are broken,” Mancuso said. “There’s too much information. We still want a high standard, but it should be streamlined.

“Guidance is not durable,” he added. “It can be torn up immediately. What we want is more rapid authorization, so that consumers have product choices that they can choose from.”

The regulatory landscape of nicotine is similar in some ways to how cannabis is being introduced and regulated in U.S. markets, Mancuso suggested, such that the substance is legal in half of U.S. states, but there’s no federal standard, creating a “hodgepodge” of regulations.

“Regulations are hard for any business,” Mancuso said. “At the very least, it should be an even playing field, not a playing field where bad actors are in a better position than responsible companies like ours.

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5328. Officials blame aging FAA telecom gear as U.S. airspace reopens, see no link to Microsoft or AI

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 3:04 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 7:58 pm

Updated with officials’ explanation of the cause and the reopening of U.S. airspace.

The nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. commercial air travel Friday was not caused by the Microsoft 365 outage that began a day earlier, federal officials said at an evening news conference, blaming aging FAA telecom equipment that was overloaded with data.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened the news conference by raising the Microsoft outage himself. “I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft,” he said. “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy likewise ruled out a role for SMART, the FAA’s new AI traffic-planning tool, saying it isn’t connected to the core systems controllers use to track flights.

“There was no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened today,” he said.

The FAA reopened U.S. airspace at 5:15 p.m. Pacific, more than four hours after the problems began, Duffy said. He said flights would resume slowly, depending on whether airlines had crews available, and some may not depart until Saturday morning.

Microsoft confirmed in a statement that it had no indication the FAA ground stop was related to its service disruption.

Asked whether a cyberattack or “rogue AI” could be ruled out, Mullin said there was “nothing completely certain right now,” but “it appears that this was mechanically driven.” He said he could not rule out the possibility of a cyberattack but said there was “zero evidence” of one so far.

What happened: Duffy said the FAA began seeing unstable radar and communications data at air traffic control facilities across the country at 12:36 p.m. Pacific. Aging switches and routers in the agency’s telecom network “got overloaded with data” and began producing inconsistent information, he said, adding that the FAA still relies on “1980s little copper lines.”

“Our new IP switches did not go down. It’s the old hardware that went down,” he said. The FAA restored service after deploying fixes to reduce the overloading on its switches, he said.

Mullin said the overload appeared to have been triggered by new equipment the FAA was installing. As the agency put “patches into the system” and added “new equipment and new technology,” he said, it “was overwhelming the older system.” Neither official said exactly what that equipment was.

The FAA is in the middle of replacing its legacy telecom network with a modern internet-protocol network. AT&T took over the lead role on that project in August with an initial $74.3 million award, as the FAA works toward a goal of finishing by the end of 2028.

Duffy and Mullin used the briefing to press Congress for money to finish rebuilding the air traffic control system. Mullin said President Trump has declared the situation a national emergency.

The administration has asked Congress for an additional $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, AeroTime reported. Duffy said at the evening news conference that he wants $50 billion.

Earlier in the day, Mullin had said officials were looking into a possible link to SMART, including through DHS’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The FAA said Tuesday it was expanding the system to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers.

The agency describes SMART as a cloud-based system that pulls in about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths and controller staffing, to recommend flight schedules and routes. FAA specialists review its recommendations, and local facilities decide whether to act on them.

SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which denied any connection to the issue. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m. Pacific. More than 3,500 planes were in the air at the time, Duffy said. It’s the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system.

FlightAware counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled as of Friday afternoon.

#5327. Gov. Ferguson seeks $10M to help develop Eastern Wash. clean-energy hub

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 4:32 pmNovember 16, 2026 at 10:09 am

Gov. Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains. The proposal will be included in his 2027–29 capital budget.

If approved by lawmakers, the funding would support sewer, water, electrical and road infrastructure at the park.

“This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The 1,641-acre site was formerly part of the Hanford Nuclear Reservation, a sprawling federal property along the Columbia River near the Tri-Cities that is undergoing a massive environmental cleanup. Hanford was established during World War II to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project.

Mel Clark, president and CEO of the CleanTech Alliance, an industry trade group, welcomed the news as the state struggles to get clean power plugged into the grid.

“Washington needs more energy generation, more clean energy, and more manufacturing,” Clark told GeekWire via email. “We’re excited to see the Governor take action to change our last-place ranking in building new clean energy projects.”

According to the governor’s office, two projects have committed to locating at the park once infrastructure construction is complete: Atlas Agro’s low-carbon fertilizer production plant and the utility-scale Ruby Flats Solar Farm.

State officials said General Matter is also considering the location for producing advanced nuclear fuel for small reactors. That siting could potentially be beneficial for another project planned for the same area: Amazon, X-energy and Energy Northwest are developing plans for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility, a nuclear plant comprised of clustered, small reactors.

In 2024, the Norwegian company Cenate expressed interest in building a factory at the park to produce lithium-ion battery components, according to the Tri-Cities Area Journal of Business, ultimately withdrew its plans.

The Tri-Cities is also attracting fusion-energy investment. Last year, Seattle startup Avalanche Energy landed a $10 million grant from the Washington State Department of Commerce’s Green Jobs Grant Program to develop FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies. The project is being developed in an existing Port of Benton building in Richland.

Washington is heading into its 2027–29 biennial budget with a multibillion-dollar shortfall, but officials have not yet settled on a definitive public estimate.

Ferguson has acknowledged the scale of the gap but has not publicly specified an amount. The shortfall concerns the state’s operating budget, which is separate from the capital budget funding proposed for the energy park.

Editor’s note: Comment from CleanTech Alliance President and CEO Mel Clark added 11/16.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5326. ‘Wolf of Wall Street’ Jordan Belfort on his AI salespeople who are better than humans: ‘What if you have a bad apple that says stuff?’

Just months after Jordan Belfort’s court-ordered restitution obligation ended, leaving his victims far short of the $110 million he was ordered to pay them, “The Wolf of Wall Street” is selling over the phone again, this time with AI bots trained on his sales techniques.

Belfort’s new AI sales-voice startup, Tone, has brought in about $1 million in revenue so far, and he’s aiming for between $20 million and $30 million in recurring revenue within the next year.

Belfort said Tone’s technology is more reliable than humans because companies can keep a firm grip on what it says. This contrasts with salespeople who can stray from approved scripts and could potentially cross a line with customers.

“What if you have a bad apple that says stuff—maybe inadvertently even, right?” he said.

Tone launched publicly on Nov. 16 with about $10 million raised, and Belfort said its API and a content creation platform goes live in about a week. It arrives as big companies move to automate customer calls—Verizon CEO Dan Schulman told Fortune this month the telecom giant is preparing to automate much of its routine customer service work—and two years after the FCC put AI-generated voices under federal robocall rules. A study by international cloud voice software company AVOXI found in September that just over half of organizations are already using AI voice agents, and a majority are planning to adopt them over the next two years.

Tone’s offerings include 16 different male and female artificial voices ranging from higher to lower-pitched that are trained on Belfort’s tonal sales techniques. Unlike other AI voices, he said they adjust their intonation and volume, among other factors, to try to better influence listeners.

This includes phrasing declarative statements as questions to show the listener you’re engaged, or speaking in a low voice to convey scarcity and the importance of the information, Belfort told Fortune. Those subtle vocal techniques, he argued, can make the difference between someone listening to a sales pitch or hanging up and will help the company compete against an increasingly crowded field of voice AI startups. The tech is not meant to replace salespeople but merely to expand the number of contacts they can reach, he added.

Of the $10 million the company has raised (TechCrunch first reported the figure), 70% of it came from friends and family and the rest from investors, he estimated.

Yet Belfort also noted that Tone still has limitations, especially when it comes to navigating complicated conversations.

To make conversations sound natural, Tone’s models have to respond within about 500 to 600 milliseconds. But that leaves only about 100 milliseconds for the AI to process a question and formulate an answer, which means the company is limited in the complexity of the models it can use to get the fastest response.

As AI models improve and computer chips become faster, however, Belfort believes that trade-off will become less significant.

“I would think in the next six months, at the most a year, that gap will be eliminated,” he said.

Belfort pleaded guilty and was later sentenced in 2003 for fraud and money laundering, spending 22 months in prison before being released in 2006. Since then, he has focused on motivational speaking and consulting. His memoir, “The Wolf of Wall Street,” also inspired the 2013 film by the same name starring Leonardo DiCaprio.

Belfort was ordered by a federal judge in 2003 to pay $110 million in restitution, yet his court-ordered restitution obligation ended earlier this year, with TMZ reporting that his victims ultimately received a much lower amount than expected. As of 2018, Belfort had paid about $13 million of the total sum, according to court documents.

The prospect of AI sales bots trained on the techniques of someone convicted of fraud raises ethical questions. Belfort’s cofounder, the venture capitalist Shervin Pishevar, has also faced sexual misconduct allegations, which he denies.

There are also regulatory concerns. The Federal Communications Commission ruled in 2024 that AI-generated voices fall under existing restrictions on robocalls under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, a federal law aimed at protecting consumers from unwanted telemarketing calls. The rules include exemptions for some noncommercial polling and survey calls to residential landlines.

Belfort previously told TechCrunch that Tone makes outbound sales calls only to opted-in leads or existing customers. The company always recommends disclosing when customers are speaking to AI, he told Fortune.

“I think it’s important that it should be disclosed, and I think the worst thing you’d want to break trust with someone—if they do at some point realize it, that would be, I think, a really bad thing,” he said.

For now, Tone offers two languages, English and Spanish, but Belfort said it plans to add two to four more languages each month. In the future, he said Tone will develop AI-powered avatars to add virutal body language and facial expressions to its portfolio of persuasion tools during video calls.

Despite his prior conviction, Belfort said he has spent the last two decades working to rebuild his reputation and is now working 14 hour days to build Tone.

“I think that the company and the technology should speak for itself, and I think people need to make their own decision,” he said.

Role: Reporter Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez is a reporter for Fortune covering general business news.

#5325. This 76-Year-Old Billionaire Built a Fortune. Now, He’s Relentlessly Pursuing Another Goal: ‘I Might Live Forever’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The billionaire never checks his email and tightly controls his calendar.

Can you micromanage your way to a longer life? This billionaire is trying.

Larry Connor is the founder and managing partner of The Connor Group, a real estate firm with over $5 billion in assets. The 76-year-old executive optimizes his schedule to make every moment matter, according to a recent report in The Wall Street Journal. He is worth $2.1 billion at the time of writing, per Forbes.

For one, Connor employs a team of about 15 individuals, including personal trainers, yoga teachers and massage therapists, who help him stay physically fit. He also keeps at least three doctors on speed dial and regularly meets with a performance coach who works with NBA and NFL players.

Connor is proud of his health. He showed the Journal a chart tracking the decline in his cholesterol over the past decade. He is adventurous and has gone on trips like a trek through the Alaskan wilderness. In 2022, he piloted a historic private mission to the International Space Station, which cost tens of millions of dollars and involved research on heart health and how cells age in space.

Connor’s staff handles his schedule and coordinates his healthcare through an internal team called the LSC Department, named for his initials. This year, he will undergo 68 tests at the Mayo Clinic, including a full-body MRI and a detailed brain scan. He has donated more than $15 million to the clinic, mostly to support aging research.

Connor estimated that his annual health costs were around $30,000. A staff member corrected him, putting the total closer to $100,000 before staff salaries, per the Journal.

Connor is intentional about what he spends his time on. The Journal revealed that he doesn’t respond to emails. His colleagues screen his messages, print them out and craft responses for him.

This makes him somewhat unusual. Former Apple CEO Tim Cook, who retired earlier this year, said in 2023 that he typically woke up at 3:45 a.m. and began his day by reading hundreds of customer emails.

“I can control the morning better than the evening and through the day. Things happen through the day that kind of blow you off course,” Cook told the Australian Financial Review in 2021. “The morning is yours. Or should I say, the early morning is yours.”

Connor takes managing his day a step further by sectioning his time into intervals as short as five minutes. That’s how he squeezes squash matches, yoga and high-intensity exercise into his day.

He often finishes his day by exercising in his office’s lobby gym. During one session this fall, a trainer led him through treadmill intervals and two rounds of strength training.

Before stretching, Connor asked for an extra workout. He had started work at 7:45 a.m. Nearly 12 hours later, he was still there.

“He’ll often say, like, ‘Hey, I might live forever,’” Ryan Ernst, Connor’s colleague who runs his philanthropic work, said in an interview with the Journal. “And sometimes I think that’s what he’s kind of planning on.”

#5323. He Took Over Burger King’s U.S. Business at 34 With No Restaurant Experience. Here’s the Question He Learned to Ask Before Launching Anything New.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Watch now to hear why Alex Macedo benched the King mascot, what a flopped menu launch taught him about franchisees and how he scales regional chains at Authentic Restaurant Brands.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Alex Macedo knew how to get people talking about Burger King. At 34, when he became president of its U.S. business, he had to learn what it took for franchisees to deliver on the promises his marketing made. Today, Macedo is the co-founder and CEO of Authentic Restaurant Brands.

Macedo had worked in consumer goods, including beer, and had some success in marketing at other businesses backed by the private equity group that bought Burger King. He joined the chain as head of marketing. He was appointed president shortly afterward.

“I was the perfect candidate,” Macedo jokes. He’d never worked in restaurants, in franchising or in the U.S. He remembers franchisees being nervous about his appointment.

As head of marketing, Macedo had benched the King mascot to help the chain appeal to more people, including older customers and women. “The King is a polarizing character,” he says. As president, he brought him back for a handful of appearances, including a walkout with Floyd Mayweather and a visit to the Kentucky Derby.

A push to rebrand the chain also involved launching several menu items at once. The team gave them funky names and expected big things. “And they didn’t work,” Macedo says.

Three new items were manageable in a test kitchen. Across a franchise system, each operator had to train crews to make all three while keeping orders moving. A nine-minute drive-thru wait could spoil a meal before a customer took a bite.

“When I started working at restaurants, the product is everything,” Macedo says.

He learned to judge new ideas by whether franchisees could carry them out and make money doing it. That meant putting more emphasis on what brought customers to Burger King in the first place, including the Whopper, and on how quickly and consistently crews could serve it.

“We had five fantastic years,” Macedo says. He recalls franchisee profitability rising and Burger King going from closing restaurants to opening new ones.

By the time he left Burger King, some of the same franchisees who’d wondered how a marketing executive would lead their restaurants were inviting him to stay in their homes. He’d learned the business from the people he’d been hired to lead.

Macedo looks for the kind of restaurant people swear by. It’s the place they keep going back to, the one where they feel so welcome it’s “like it’s your second home.” At Authentic Restaurant Brands, that feeling is part of what makes a regional chain worth buying.

“They are loved, right?” Macedo says. “Their Google scores are the highest, their engagement scores are the highest, their reviews are the highest, their NPS is the highest.”

He also looks for strong sales and margins. A restaurant can mean a lot to its regulars and still be a difficult business to run. Macedo wants to see both kinds of evidence: that people care about the place and that enough of them come back to sustain it.

Tavern in the Square, a casual dining chain, was already doing about $7.5 million in sales per restaurant when Authentic Restaurant Brands bought it, Macedo says. It had reached that volume without a loyalty program. His team brought in a provider it uses across the portfolio, and Tavern got its own program. The operators liked the point-of-sale system they already had, so they kept it. By the time of the interview, Macedo says, sales had risen to about $8.6 million per restaurant, and the four newest locations were tracking above $10.5 million each.

The same thinking extends to the food. Authentic Restaurant Brands can buy insurance together, but chicken purchasing is left to the individual chains. Each has its own specifications, and Macedo doesn’t want a bulk discount tempting anyone to change them. He says he’d “prefer to serve better food the way that people have always done.”

For Macedo, part of buying a restaurant people love is knowing which decisions to leave with the team that earned that loyalty. A new rewards program can give regulars another reason to come back. When they do, they’re still coming back for the place they knew.

#5322. Microsoft’s Satya Nadella praises Jensen Huang, says return as CEO is ‘up to the Nvidia board’

Microsoft Chief Executive Satya Nadella praised ousted Nvidia founder Jensen Huang as “a singular person” who has contributed immensely to the tech industry, but he stopped short of calling for Huang’s reinstatement to the chipmaker’s top job.

“I just want to give him space for what he needs to do there, and it’s not up to me. It’s up to the Nvidia board to decide what happens next,” Nadella said Tuesday at a media roundtable in San Francisco during Microsoft’s Ignite conference. He added that he had “all the admiration, respect for what Jensen has done for this industry, and what he’s done for Nvidia,” noting that he has known and worked with Huang for a long time.

Huang, who turned Nvidia into the dominant maker of AI chips and owns about a 3.56% stake, on Thursday stepped down as CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago, amid revelations of multiple affairs, including one with an executive whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese spy. On Tuesday morning, Huang broke his silence and said he would be open to returning as CEO. Later in the day, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the company did not intend to bring Huang back.

Nadella, who said he texted Huang over the weekend to say he was thinking of him, said that Nvidia has a deep bench of talent.

“I think Nvidia does have a lot of human capital and very capable leadership,” Nadella said, noting that interim CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress once worked at Microsoft. “I’m making sure that we have the same type of partnership, and we’re scaling Rubins as we speak,” Nadella said, referring to Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin line of processors. “It’s a pretty critical project for us.”

As one of the world’s largest cloud computing providers, Microsoft is a major purchaser of Nvidia chips, and the two companies have a longstanding relationship. Nadella appeared with Huang last month at a Microsoft Windows event.

Nvidia is navigating its most tumultuous period in company history, as Huang’s ouster has raised numerous questions about how one of the world’s most valuable companies can continue to operate without the all-powerful executive who was critical to its decision-making and deals, including agreements with Microsoft and other major tech companies.

Speaking about the recent midterm elections and the overwhelming rejection of AI data centers by communities throughout the U.S. that voted to restrict data center development, Nadella said that building data centers requires earning support “one community at a time” by delivering long-term local value, rather than attempting to lobby in Washington. He acknowledged community skepticism, such as concerns that data centers create local nuisances or drive up electricity bills, and emphasized that companies cannot resolve this through public relations alone, but must physically prove the benefits.

“I don’t think the public is getting it wrong,” he said. Nadella also stated that election results have not altered Microsoft’s plans for building data centers, and he noted that the constraints on data center growth are more about the availability of power, chip wafers, and memory, rather than election cycles.

Nadella also addressed a massive outage of Microsoft’s systems last week that disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot, SharePoint, and other Microsoft 365 services worldwide. And he spoke about the company’s recent buyout offer to 60,000 employees, which is nearly 30% of its workforce.

Nadella said that the outage was not caused by AI code or AI deployments, and that the incident was a “perfect storm” in which a bug surfaced under specific web traffic conditions during routine testing. In fact, internal AI tools helped engineers solve the problem more quickly, he said.

Nadella said that the voluntary buyout offers were designed for employees to “have some agency on how they decide what to do with their careers,” and that rather than leaving employees with the anxiety of something happening to their jobs, the offers gave people a clear option. He did not say whether the offers were a prelude to layoffs.

“There are some teams that are changing faster, some teams that are in a different place,” he said, speaking about the different speeds of teams that are part of the company’s workplace transformation.

#5321. ‘I hope this email finds you’: Microsoft declares outage over as the world digs out of its inbox

by Todd Bishop on Nov 14, 2026 at 10:35 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:28 am

Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.

“Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.

Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote.

Microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The company says the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details.

The company said late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log. Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal.

A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user, he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five.

In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud.

Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth.

Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto, a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health said patient care continued without disruption.

In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported, citing Nikkei.

In New York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems, including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email.

About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Microsoft itself looked to preempt the speculation a few hours earlier, posting on X that it had “no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.”

The Microsoft 365 outage was at least the fourth significant one this year. A January outage lasted nearly 10 hours, and in July a bug in Microsoft’s automated network maintenance system disrupted Azure and Microsoft 365 services for hours. On Aug. 31, an Exchange Online outage also hit Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint.

Instead of “I hope this email finds you well,” many people joked, it should just be “I hope this email finds you.” (Consider this our nomination for the “Overworked Twitter Joke of the Week” on The Ringer’s Press Box podcast.)

Microsoft said Friday afternoon that it was watching the backlog of delayed email “to ensure all process successfully before considering the issue resolved.” The University of Washington’s IT department told its users that email delayed during the outage would be delivered as mail queues continued to be processed.

Many people coped with the flood of returning email with a bit of levity.

As the mail started flowing again, CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter said he was getting “a deluge of emails from PR people pitching their clients to talk about the Outlook outage.” Most were sent during the outage, he noted, “which, fittingly, prevented the pitches from reaching me.”

The security company Malwarebytes captured the paradox in a message to its followers: “We regret to inform you that Teams and Outlook are coming back online after a global outage.”

#5320. 5 Things to Consider Before Leaving Your Career to Start a Business

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Starting a business can offer greater independence and new opportunities, but making the transition successfully requires more than a good idea.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For many professionals, the idea of starting a business begins with a simple question: What if I worked for myself?

Perhaps you’ve spent years building someone else’s business, reached a point where career advancement feels limited or simply want more control over your professional future. Whatever the motivation, entrepreneurship can be an exciting next chapter. But enthusiasm alone isn’t enough to build a sustainable business.

Before handing in your resignation, consider these five factors that can help you make a more informed transition.

One of the biggest misconceptions about entrepreneurship is that you need an entirely new set of skills to start a business. Many of the abilities you’ve developed throughout your career may translate directly into business ownership.

Even if your previous career has little connection to the industry you’re considering, these transferable skills can provide a meaningful foundation.

The key is recognizing what you already bring to the table — and identifying where additional training or experience may be needed.

Not every business requires a storefront, employees, inventory or a large upfront investment. Today’s entrepreneurs can choose from a variety of business models, including consulting, professional services, online businesses and relationship-driven industries.

Before committing to an opportunity, ask yourself:

It’s also important to distinguish between owning a business and simply creating another demanding job for yourself.

A business model that looks attractive on paper may not be the right fit for your personality, financial situation or long-term goals.

Starting a business involves more than calculating the initial investment.

There may be expenses for training, technology, marketing, insurance, professional services and everyday operations. Some businesses also require ongoing spending before they begin generating consistent revenue. Equally important is understanding your personal financial obligations.

Consider creating a realistic budget that accounts for:

Don’t assume that revenue will arrive immediately or consistently. A thoughtful financial plan can help you make decisions based on realistic expectations rather than unnecessary pressure.

Entrepreneurs often focus on what they need to know. But who they know — and the relationships they develop — can be equally important.

Depending on the industry, relationships with suppliers, professional advisers, referral partners, customers and other business owners can create opportunities that would be difficult to develop independently.

Strong business relationships aren’t built simply by collecting contacts. They require trust, reliability, communication and a willingness to provide value.

As you explore a new business, consider which professional relationships you’ll need and how you’ll begin developing them. You may also benefit from experienced mentors who understand the challenges of operating in your chosen industry.

While mentorship doesn’t eliminate the difficulties of entrepreneurship, it can provide perspective when you’re facing unfamiliar decisions.

One of the most overlooked aspects of starting a business is customer acquisition.

It’s easy to become absorbed in choosing a company name, designing a logo, creating a website or setting up an office. Those activities may be necessary, but none guarantees that customers will find you.

Before launching, think carefully about how you intend to generate business.

Marketing should be part of your business plan from the beginning, not something you figure out after opening your doors.

A clear strategy for reaching potential customers can help you prioritize your time, spending and daily activities.

Leaving an established career to start a business is a significant decision, and there’s no single path that works for everyone.

Some entrepreneurs transition gradually while maintaining their current employment. Others decide to make a complete career change after carefully evaluating their financial position and business opportunity.

Neither approach guarantees success. What matters is understanding the responsibilities of business ownership, choosing an opportunity that fits your circumstances and developing a realistic plan for moving forward.

Entrepreneurship isn’t simply about leaving a job. It’s about taking responsibility for building something of your own. And the more thoughtfully you prepare for that transition, the better equipped you’ll be to navigate the challenges and opportunities ahead.
