#5319. Yum China CEO Joey Wat: What China’s consumer market can teach global business

Joey Wat is the CEO of Yum China, the largest restaurant company in China by system sales. The company operates around 20,000 stores across six brands in China, including KFC, Pizza Hut and Lavazza.

In 1987, KFC opened its first restaurant in Beijing, marking the debut of China’s first Western quick-service restaurant brand. Nearly four decades later, KFC China has expanded to more than 14,000 stores in a market that has transformed around it.

KFC has changed alongside it. In addition to the Original Recipe Chicken and Zinger, our menu offers energy bowls and sparkling coffee – many of which cannot be found in KFC menus outside China. More broadly, we have adapted everything from marketing to store formats as consumer preferences, technology and competition have evolved.

For any global brand, keeping pace with such change requires tremendous effort. I believe one reason KFC has been able to keep adapting is the strength of our local teams. They have the know-how and autonomy to respond to the market with agility. The brand may be global, but decisions are made close to the consumer.

KFC is one of the six restaurant brands operated by Yum China, which together span 20,000 stores across the country. Our experience, including 10 years as a company listed on the New York Stock Exchange, has reinforced three lessons for global brands seeking to win in this market. While shaped in China, I believe they extend far beyond it.

One fundamental reality about China is that it is not a single market, but many. Consumer preferences, consumption occasions and competitive landscapes vary across regions and city tiers. A single playbook is not enough to win, which is why we tailor store formats and menus for select lower-tier cities. Yet highly tailored solutions can be costly, making a dual focus on innovation and efficiency essential.

Yum China’s 20,000-store portfolio gives us a strong platform. Two years ago, we began carving out space within existing KFC stores for side-by-side modules such as KCOFFEE cafés to tap into fast-growing coffee demand. Since then, KCOFFEE cafes have expanded to over 4,000 locations, driving incremental sales and profit without incurring the investment of a new store. We have also extended this approach to KFC’s KPRO and Pizza Hut’s Burger Bar to capture the emerging light meal and the large burger market respectively.

Consumers look for exciting new products and great value. We meet those needs by launching 500-600 new or upgraded products a year across our brands. To make this both efficient and sustainable, we draw inspiration from hero products to launch innovations such as the Intriguing Oreo Original Recipe Chicken Burger and Pizza Dough Burgers. As we drive transaction growth and tap into smaller-order occasions, we have been able to sustain the margins. Doing so requires transformation across nearly every part of the business, from supply chain and operations to technology.

This is why innovation and efficiency can reinforce each other: innovative solutions drive efficiency, and efficiency in turn creates room for further innovations.

In fast-moving markets, there is constant pressure to focus on visible results. But resilience in challenging times requires investment in capabilities whose value may not be immediately apparent.

I often think of bamboo, common across southern China, including my hometown in Fujian Province. Its strength lies underground, in roots that grow deep and wide, forming a complex, mutually reinforcing web. When green shoots finally emerge, they can grow with astonishing speed and become a forest that can weather storms.

A business follows a similar pattern. The capabilities that make scale possible are often invisible for years. At Yum China, we have invested patiently in a root system: supply chain, digital and membership ecosystems, food innovation and organizational strength.

These capabilities allow new concepts to draw on systems that have been built and strengthened over decades, rather than starting from scratch.

Bamboo teaches us patience and discipline. Invest in the foundation, and trust that scale will follow. It also reminds us that success is interconnected. Like the roots of a forest, strong businesses reinforce one another.

When I was 15, I worked part-time as a restaurant food runner. It taught me the dignity of hard work and the importance of frontline employees.

That experience shaped a belief I still hold today: employees come first, followed by customers and shareholders. This may sound like sacrilege to some, particularly for a public company, but it is essential to creating sustainable long-term value. Take care of employees, who shape customer experiences. Customers enable business performance. Business performance ultimately drives shareholder returns.

Frontline employees often see changes in consumer sentiment and behavior early. They spot problems before they appear on dashboards. Having the right strategy is important, but without the right people to execute it, it cannot succeed. Put simply, execution is growth.

This people-first mindset matters even more in the age of AI. AI can help forecast demand and optimize staffing. But these systems are only effective when they are built on the knowledge and judgment of experienced operators.

As agentic AI begins to reshape how companies operate, one of the most undervalued assets in any organization may be its experienced operators – the “old masters” who understand the business deeply and can guide the integration of new technology into real workflows. Technology alone does not create advantage. People who know how to apply it do.

The same lesson applies to global companies seeking to sustain success in China. Many strong local companies are founder-led. They move with speed, focus and entrepreneurial conviction. To compete effectively, multinational companies need local teams with good judgment and enough autonomy to respond just as quickly.

China’s lesson for U.S. business leaders is clear: brand heritage can open doors and global scale can create powerful advantages. But both become liabilities if they breed complacency or slow decision-making.

The real test is not whether a company can succeed in a market once. It is whether it can keep adapting as consumers and technology evolve. It is no longer enough for leaders to see where the future is headed. The best leaders build organizations capable of riding on the opportunities and challenges.

#5318. Who should run Nvidia? Our picks for Jensen Huang’s successor, whether the board likes it or not

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 14, 2026 at 2:10 pmNovember 14, 2026 at 2:10 pm

Nvidia’s board says it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang. Sorry, we’re having too much fun coming up with names.

The board said in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates. That came after the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas — a name John had presciently floated when we recorded this week’s GeekWire Podcast on Thursday.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Colette Kress, the company’s longtime CFO, is serving as interim CEO. She spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to run a deliberate search that leaves open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Elon Musk said on X that he was signing a petition to reinstate Huang.

The organizers of one, called “Stand with Jensen,” say it has more than 108,000 names, including more than 5,600 people who identify themselves as current Nvidia employees.

The case for Haas: The Arm CEO spent about seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in February 2022, when Nvidia’s $40 billion deal to acquire Arm collapsed amid regulatory opposition. SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, kept Nvidia’s $1.25 billion prepayment.

Arm, based in Cambridge, England, designs processor technology that’s ubiquitous in smartphones, and licenses it to other chipmakers. That includes Nvidia, whose Grace data center CPU, paired with its GPUs in AI systems, is built on Arm cores. Amazon’s Graviton and Microsoft’s Cobalt server chips also use Arm designs.

Haas is one of several candidates, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be offered the job or take it, the FT reported.

He also has a link to Harvey Jones, the longtime Nvidia director named the company’s first board chair this week. Haas was vice president of sales at Tensilica, a chip-design company, from 1999 to 2004, according to his LinkedIn profile. Jones co-founded Tensilica and chaired its board until chip-design software maker Cadence acquired it in 2013.

Haas has also seen Huang’s resistance to succession planning firsthand. “He didn’t like the idea,” Haas said in a 2024 interview, as quoted by the New York Times this week. “He felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.”

One complication: SoftBank named Haas CEO of SoftBank Group International in April, helping coordinate chip and AI companies in its international portfolio while he continues to run Arm. The FT reported that the appointment was aimed at pushing forward Project Izanagi, SoftBank’s AI chip effort launched to compete with Nvidia.

He knows Nvidia from the inside, but he also knows what it’s like to run a public company — which matters for a board searching in the middle of a crisis.

John’s argument on the podcast: Nvidia needs someone who can shepherd a company through turmoil, not just a great technologist. Think Alan Mulally going from Boeing to Ford, or Dara Khosrowshahi moving from Expedia to Uber after Travis Kalanick’s ouster.

What the betting markets say: On Kalshi, Ian Buck, the Nvidia vice president who created the CUDA software platform, was the favorite at midday Friday. By midday Saturday, Haas had overtaken him, at 25% to Buck’s 18%. Kress was at 10%.

The Axios list of 11 names also includes Apple Executive Chair Tim Cook, for whom President Trump lobbied on Truth Social (“A Legend replaces a Legend!”), along with AMD CEO Lisa Su and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian.

A Northwest wildcard: Analysts have also floated Sanjay Mehrotra, CEO of Boise, Idaho-based Micron Technology, whose memory chips power Nvidia’s AI servers. Mehrotra co-founded SanDisk in 1988 and has run Micron since 2017.

The AWS chief: Matt Garman has run Amazon Web Services since June 2024, overseeing a business with a $142 billion annual revenue run rate at the end of last year. He started at Amazon as an MBA intern in 2005, joined AWS full time in 2006 as one of its first product managers, and later led its compute business and then its sales and marketing organization.

Another Amazon pick: We’d also look at Peter DeSantis, who now leads a new organization that includes Amazon’s AI models, custom chips and quantum computing, reporting directly to CEO Andy Jassy.

DeSantis joined Amazon as a software developer in 1998. He led the EC2 team from Cape Town, South Africa, through its 2006 launch, and spearheaded Amazon’s 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs, the Israeli chip designer behind its custom silicon.

In 2018, DeSantis unveiled Graviton. In June, he told Bloomberg that AWS was in talks to sell its Trainium AI chips to other companies for their own data centers.

He knows chips, data centers and AI infrastructure at enormous scale. The catch, as John noted: he’s never been a CEO, and the board may want that experience given the circumstances.

The other Amazon name: Dave Treadwell took over AWS compute and machine learning services in August. Treadwell spent 27 years at Microsoft, where he worked on Windows NT, .NET and Xbox and rose to corporate vice president, before joining Amazon in 2016.

The Microsoft bench: On the podcast, Todd ran through a few Microsoft executives who would bring relevant experience:

The insider with Microsoft roots: Nick Parker, a 26-year Microsoft sales veteran, joined Nvidia in August as executive vice president of worldwide field operations, with a pay package worth more than $40 million. He’s new, but he already runs the team that sells Nvidia’s chips to the world’s largest companies.

One more angle: Whoever gets the job will face a growing list of customers trying to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, including Amazon. In his annual shareholder letter in April, Jassy wrote that Amazon’s chips business would have an annual run rate of about $50 billion if it sold chips to AWS and other third parties the way other chipmakers do.

Jassy said it’s “quite possible” Amazon will sell racks of them to third parties in the future.

In a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14, Huang said he hoped his successor was already inside the company. The board has said it will consider both internal and external candidates.

Listen to our full discussion on this week’s GeekWire Podcast.

#5317. Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party."

The most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division said it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

The staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

That phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

This is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself says the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the issues presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

In practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

For a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

The framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

That sequence matters. The interpretation says what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

For now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

#5316. How to Make Clipping Work in Your Marketing Strategy

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Clipping turns your podcasts and keynotes into hundreds of short-form posts across social media, and it’s one of the most cost-efficient marketing channels most brands still aren’t using.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Nobody wants to sit through a two-hour keynote anymore. I don’t, and I’m guessing you don’t either. What people will watch is the 40-second clip of the one moment that mattered. That shift in how we consume content is why clipping has become one of the most cost-efficient ways to market a brand right now. It’s also one of the most misunderstood.

Clipping started in streaming about three years ago. Music picked it up next, the way music picks up every new marketing method first. Then TV and film distributors got into it, then direct-to-consumer brands, and now B2B companies, including some of the biggest names in fintech and enterprise software. Even so, most marketing teams I talk to still aren’t sure what it is or where it fits.

Most people already understand influencers and UGC creators. They use their own face and record their own content. A clipper is different. A clipper runs their own social media page on Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or X, but instead of making something from scratch, they take content that already exists, pick the moment they think will hit and cut it down into a short clip for their page. The content is already there. The clipper’s job is getting it seen.

So as a brand, you hand over your long-form content. Maybe that’s an hour-long podcast episode or a conference keynote. Clippers cut it into short pieces, post them on their own accounts and get paid based on views. Right now that’s usually somewhere between $1 and $5 for every thousand views.

When you scroll social media, around 10% of what you see is an ad, and it’s labeled as an ad. The other 90% is organic content. You can run ads, but that only gets you a small slice of the time people spend on these apps. If you want the rest, you need organic content and a lot of it.

That’s where clipping comes in. Instead of deciding in a conference room which moment from that podcast will hit, you put the content in the hands of clippers, each of whom picks their own moments. You end up with hundreds of different cuts in the span of four to eight hours, and the algorithm decides what works best. That’s A/B testing at a speed no internal team can match.

Clipping can’t save bad content. If people don’t want to watch it, putting it in front of more of them doesn’t help.

The easiest way to figure out what good content looks like is to go see what your competitors and the brands you look up to are posting. Then mimic it and improve it.

When you do that research, don’t trust third-party data. Don’t go on ChatGPT and ask what the top people in your industry are making content about, because then you end up making the exact same content everybody else is posting. You need first-party data. Go on YouTube, search it up and look with your own eyes. If you do it, you’re already doing what everybody else isn’t, and that’s an edge.

People don’t purchase from brands. They purchase from people. So either you become the ambassador for your brand, or you put the right ambassadors in front of it and have them help you make the content.

That’s why I tell brands not to stop doing UGC just because they started clipping. Keep doing UGC. And instead of only paying for short-form clips, pay someone in your space who has real authority to make a long-form video, maybe 10 or 15 minutes. Then feed that into your clipping campaigns too.

Keep it raw. People don’t want the perfect, super official, branded clip. They want something that looks organic and doesn’t feel like it’s trying to sell them something every second. People hate being sold to.

Before you launch a campaign, decide what it’s for. Awareness and conversion are different campaigns. For most brands, clipping is about awareness. It gets more people hearing about you, and it’s one more touchpoint in the mix alongside your ads, your creators and your influencers.

Once you see clips working, milk them. I’ve had clients tell me they’re seeing the same clip posted too many times and they want more variation. Think about it like ads. If you’ve tested 10 different creatives and one is doing really well, do you stop it and go make more variations? No. You keep putting money behind it. With clipping, you double down by having more accounts post that same clip. That’s how you get that feeling of being everywhere, so don’t be afraid of it.

Not every clipping partner is the same, and the wrong one can hurt your brand. Here’s what I’d look for.

Attention spans keep going down; everyone is competing for the same eyeballs, and CPMs on ads are only going up. Clipping won’t replace the rest of your marketing, but it’s one of the most cost-efficient ways to get your best moments in front of a lot more people. Right now, that’s an arbitrage opportunity most brands are still sleeping on.

Nobody wants to sit through a two-hour keynote anymore. I don’t, and I’m guessing you don’t either. What people will watch is the 40-second clip of the one moment that mattered. That shift in how we consume content is why clipping has become one of the most cost-efficient ways to market a brand right now. It’s also one of the most misunderstood.

Clipping started in streaming about three years ago. Music picked it up next, the way music picks up every new marketing method first. Then TV and film distributors got into it, then direct-to-consumer brands, and now B2B companies, including some of the biggest names in fintech and enterprise software. Even so, most marketing teams I talk to still aren’t sure what it is or where it fits.

Most people already understand influencers and UGC creators. They use their own face and record their own content. A clipper is different. A clipper runs their own social media page on Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or X, but instead of making something from scratch, they take content that already exists, pick the moment they think will hit and cut it down into a short clip for their page. The content is already there. The clipper’s job is getting it seen.

#5315. Nvidia chair closes the door on Jensen Huang comeback; analysts don’t push on China/Singapore black box

Nvidia’s board ended the talk of a Jensen Huang comeback on Tuesday. On the company’s first earnings call without its cofounder, chair Harvey Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” He then ruled out any discussion of why Huang left.

“We will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation,” Jones said. None of the eight analysts who got on the line pressed the point. None asked about Singapore or Megaspeed or about a report earlier Tuesday that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating whether Nvidia misled investors. It was a bit tense.

That left the biggest open question about the world’s biggest chipmaker unasked: where some of its revenue really ends up. Nvidia beat Wall Street’s estimates by about $7 billion on $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, as Fortune’s Alexei Oreskovic reported. Nvidia stock was up nearly 5% in after-hours trading to roughly $163.

Jones said Huang “voluntarily resigned” on Nov. 12 “after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” The board accepted the resignation unanimously, he said. It has hired a search firm and will consider internal and external candidates.

Huang had said earlier Tuesday on X that he “would be honored” to return as CEO. “I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he wrote.

Jones tied the search to the national security questions around the company. “Our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully,” he said. On Tuesday the board also created a national security and export control oversight committee. Jones said it “will enhance our engagement with the U.S. government, including all relevant agencies.”

The call had a one-question limit. Bank of America’s Vivek Arya came closest to the scandal, asking about talent retention and the leadership transition. Interim CEO Colette Kress said that among employees, “there are diverse opinions,” and that “from a business perspective, it’s business as usual.” Other analysts asked about margins, vendor financing and next year’s outlook.

The question they skipped is a downright national-security scandal. In the quarter that ended July 2025, Nvidia attributed $10.2 billion in sales, 22% of its revenue, to customers billed in Singapore, according to its 10-Q filing. “Customers use Singapore to centralize invoicing while our products are almost always shipped elsewhere,” the company wrote in that filing. It added that over 99% of its controlled data center compute revenue billed to Singapore was for orders from U.S.-based customers.

The next quarter, Nvidia began reporting revenue by the location of customers’ headquarters. It said that change “provides a better representation of the geographic profile of our revenue.” Singapore no longer appears as a line.

On Monday, the Commerce and Justice departments confirmed a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company suspected of helping shift Nvidia’s most powerful technology to China, according to AFP. Commerce began probing the company in 2024. The departments said Nvidia put Megaspeed on a “no sell” list in June 2025. Huang resigned after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. She is not related to him. Megaspeed has said it will work “constructively” with the government.

On Tuesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the SEC is opening a civil probe into whether Nvidia’s disclosures misled investors.

Kress gave one new China detail: sales of licensed Hopper data center chips to China were $2.4 billion in the quarter. “We are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China,” she said. The company’s forecast for next quarter assumes no data center compute revenue from China.

On new Commerce Department export rules released this week, which tighten access to advanced chips through other countries, Kress said Nvidia is “still going to spend some time studying those.” She also said “demand far exceeding supply” would keep performance strong. Nvidia raised its outlook for fiscal 2028 revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%.

Kress also put a number on customer concentration: frontier AI labs are expected to make up about 15% of Nvidia’s data center revenue this year.

Kress said Nvidia will file its 10-Q “in the coming weeks,” the first regional revenue breakdown since Huang’s exit. Huang and general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to transcribed interviews with three House committees, and Huang’s is expected before Thanksgiving. Kress ended the call with: “We’ve got this.”

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5313. You Can’t Build a Culture of Innovation If You’re the Only One Making Decisions. Here’s How to Empower Your Team.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Here’s how to give teams the confidence and capacity to turn good ideas into meaningful improvements.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

An employee spots a problem customers keep running into. She proposes a small change, explains how she would test it and sends it to her manager. The manager likes the idea but wants the founder’s approval.

Two weeks later, it’s still waiting. At the next company meeting, the founder asks everyone to be more innovative.

This is an easy contradiction to miss when you’re running a growing business. You want people to take initiative, but you also want visibility into decisions. You hire capable employees, but keep approval processes built back when you knew every customer and reviewed every expense.

Eventually, people adjust. They stop bringing you ideas that take too much effort to get approved. They focus on the work they know they can finish.

As founder of ButterflyMX, I’ve learned that a culture of innovation depends on what happens between someone noticing an opportunity and being able to act on it. Leaders shape that experience through the decisions they delegate, the time they protect and the way they respond when an experiment disappoints.

Before launching another initiative to encourage creativity, look at the last few improvements employees suggested.

What happened to them? Did anyone have the authority to move them forward? Was there time to do the work? Did the person who raised the idea ever hear why it was accepted, postponed or rejected?

Imagine a support team repeatedly answering the same question during customer onboarding. An employee suggests changing the instructions customers receive. The proposal moves through several departments, each with reasonable concerns. Nobody owns the final decision, so the instructions stay the same.

As companies grow, founders need to revisit processes that once worked well. An approval that took five minutes when everyone sat around the same table may now involve three meetings and a week of waiting.

Start by tracing a few stalled ideas through the business. Look for repeated handoffs, unclear ownership and decisions that still come to you out of habit. Fixing one of those obstacles gives employees a concrete reason to bring forward the next idea.

“Use your judgment” sounds empowering. It becomes difficult to follow when employees cannot tell which decisions will trigger a second-guessing session. Useful autonomy requires specificity.

Choose a recurring decision that your team currently brings to you. Explain what they can decide independently, what boundaries apply and what circumstances require escalation. Include the reasoning behind those boundaries so people can apply them to situations you have not anticipated.

A support manager, for example, could have authority to test revised onboarding instructions with a small group of customers. The test might need to stay within existing brand guidelines, preserve required disclosures and include a way to return to the original version. Within those limits, the manager can proceed.

The level of oversight should reflect the consequences of the decision. A limited, reversible test can move quickly. A change involving customer commitments, sensitive information or significant spending deserves more review.

Founders also have to honor the authority they delegate. If you ask employees to own a decision and then reopen it whenever you would have chosen differently, they’ll learn to check with you first.

Explain your concerns, help people improve their judgment, and allow reasonable differences in approach. Delegation only creates room for innovation when employees can rely on it.

Innovation takes time that must come from somewhere.

Employees need space to investigate recurring problems, talk to customers and test alternatives. If every hour is already committed, improvement work gets pushed into the margins. It becomes something people attempt after finishing everything else.

Ask a team which repetitive task consumes time without requiring much judgment. It might be manually assigning service requests, assembling a recurring report or entering the same information into multiple systems. Determine whether that work can be simplified, automated or stopped.

Consider a team that spends hours routing customer requests. Automating part of that process could give an employee time to examine why a particular request keeps appearing. That investigation might lead to clearer instructions, a product improvement or a change in how customers are onboarded.

When the team identifies an improvement to test, keep the experiment manageable. Define the problem, the proposed change, the person responsible and the evidence that will determine whether it helped. Set a review date. A test should be small enough to finish alongside the team’s other priorities.

This also requires leaders to say what can wait. When every existing commitment remains urgent, employees have little reason to believe experimentation is a real priority.

Employees pay close attention to what happens when a reasonable idea produces a disappointing result.

Suppose a team tests a shorter onboarding process, expecting customers to get started faster. Instead, support requests rise because customers miss information they need.

The team now has evidence about where simplification went too far. What happens next will influence whether they volunteer another idea.

A useful review examines the original hypothesis, how the test was run and what the results support. Did the team stay within the agreed boundaries? Did it notice the problem promptly? Can it explain what to retain, revise or stop?

Leaders should distinguish a disappointing result from careless execution. Ignoring agreed limits or continuing after clear warning signs requires a different response from running a thoughtful test that disproves a hypothesis.

Be equally careful about rewarding activity. A team that launches five experiments has not necessarily contributed more than a team that runs one and makes a valuable decision. Recognize clear reasoning, responsible execution and findings that other people can use.

When a test ends, share what changed, what the team learned and what happens next. That follow-through gives employees a reason to bring forward another idea, with confidence that they can act on it.

An employee spots a problem customers keep running into. She proposes a small change, explains how she would test it and sends it to her manager. The manager likes the idea but wants the founder’s approval.

Two weeks later, it’s still waiting. At the next company meeting, the founder asks everyone to be more innovative.

This is an easy contradiction to miss when you’re running a growing business. You want people to take initiative, but you also want visibility into decisions. You hire capable employees, but keep approval processes built back when you knew every customer and reviewed every expense.

#5312. To appoint the next comptroller general of the United States, follow the law

The new approach being employed to appoint the next Comptroller General of the United States should raise a red flag. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), which is headed by the Comptroller General, plays an important role in helping Congress discharge its responsibilities under Article I of the U.S. Constitution, particularly in connection with oversight of the Executive Branch.

We were shocked to learn that U.S. Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY), Chairman of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs (HSGAC), recently and spontaneously requested that names be submitted to him, under a short time constraint, to be recommended to the President for nomination as the next Comptroller General of the United States.

Under the GAO Act of 1980, a 10-member statutory bipartisan and bicameral Comptroller General Selection Commission was created. Chairman Paul is a member, since he is Chair of the HSGAC, but he is not the Chairman of the Commission. That Commission is required to jointly develop and transmit a list of at least three qualified nominees to the President. That is the law, and that is how the process of appointing the Comptroller General has been conducted since 1980.

The current vacancy for Comptroller General of the United States began on Dec. 30, 2025, and yet the Commission and its members have never met.

Equally shocking is that Sen. Paul took the liberty as HSGAC Chairman to insert an empty placeholder for an unnamed nominee for Comptroller General of the United States for a Nov. 19, 2026, Committee confirmation hearing.

Again, Sen. Paul did so even though the statutorily required Comptroller General Selection Commission has never convened or submitted a list of candidates. Then, on Nov. 16, President Trump submitted a nominee for confirmation.

The General Accounting Office Act of 1980 included a revised method for appointing the Comptroller General. It recognized that the position was in the Legislative Branch and that GAO was the primary agency the Congress uses to conduct oversight of the Executive Branch. Therefore, it provided for a bipartisan and bicameral commission to recommend candidates to the President for possible appointment.

It also provided for a 15-year non-renewable term with extremely difficult removal requirements to help ensure the independence of the Comptroller General. This 15-year term is the longest for any appointed position in the federal government.

To be clear, the 1980 law doesn’t say in so many words that the President must pick from the Commission’s list. The Senate report on the bill said he could, “in his discretion,” look elsewhere, but should give the Commission’s recommendations “great weight.” You can’t weigh a list that doesn’t exist. Every Comptroller General nominated since 1980 came from a Commission list, and the law’s answer to a President who wants other options is to ask the Commission for more names, not to skip it. Henry Wray, a former GAO attorney who helped develop the 1980 law, says the current unprecedented process “violates both the letter and the spirit of the law.”

It is extremely important for Congress to follow the statutory process. Dave Walker and Gene Dodaro (two of the coauthors of this piece) were unanimously confirmed under this process in 1998 and 2010, respectively. Both of these appointments were made under the statutory commission method, which has worked like a charm.

With regard to potential candidates, any Comptroller General should be a highly qualified executive with relevant past experience who will operate in a professional, objective, fact-based, non-partisan, non-ideological, and non-personal manner. The Comptroller General must be independent from the Executive Branch, which the GAO audits, investigates, and evaluates on behalf of the Congress and the American people. In addition, any Comptroller General must have broad bipartisan support. In fact, every one of the past eight Comptrollers General was confirmed with overwhelming bipartisan support. All of these factors are of critical importance for the Comptroller General to be credible and for him or her, and the GAO, to be effective.

Since Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Paul and President Trump have not followed the statutory requirements for the appointment of the Comptroller General, the Nov. 19, 2026, confirmation hearing should be canceled, and the normal appointment process should be adhered to.

Steve H. Hanke is a senior contributing columnist at Fortune, a professor of applied economics at The Johns Hopkins University, and a director of the Federal Fiscal Sustainability Foundation. David M. Walker is the former Comptroller General of the United States and the chairman of the Federal Fiscal Sustainability Foundation. Gene Dodaro is the former Comptroller General of the United States, who headed the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO).

#5310. Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am

The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

The window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

Competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”

The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

Momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

Jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

At AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”

Finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook says Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”

Prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”

Swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Farecast, the airfare prediction company I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments company whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, said it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one big shot once you have it.

Chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

To repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one says, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

In AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

#5309. How This Actor and Coffee Shop Owner Lives on $35K a Year in NYC: ‘I’ve Been Very Fortunate’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

She considers running her own cafe to be her side hustle.

For Sonnie Brown, every dollar counts. She’s pursuing an acting career while running a cafe on the side.

Brown is a New York resident who lives in Astoria, in the western portion of the borough of Queens. In a new interview with The New York Times, Brown offered a transparent look into her finances and shed light on her priorities.

For one, she owns a cafe in Astoria called Sonbobs Coffee House, which connects her to the neighborhood. Brown knows her regulars by name and their orders by heart. She spends long days behind the counter making coffee and catching up with her customers.

However long she spends at the cafe, Brown thinks of it as her side hustle. Her main pursuit is acting. In some years, she has landed up to five film and TV credits, along with work in commercials and theater.

Her credits include the play What You Are Now, the CBS crime drama CIA and a recurring role as a judge on Law & Order that brings her back about once a year.

Lately, acting jobs have been harder to come by. Last year, Brown earned about $35,000 from theater and television work.

“I’ve been very fortunate in the amount of work I’ve gotten,” she told the Times. “I just haven’t always been able to support myself doing it.”

Her cafe, which offers homemade muffins and sandwiches in addition to coffee, helps fill in the gaps. Brown made $90,000 through the cafe last year and spent $80,000 in operating expenses. The remaining $10,000 profit remained in the cafe’s bank account; Brown did not touch it for her personal expenses.

Brown said she pays herself by eating food from the cafe. She goes to Costco every week to source ingredients for her recipes and buys the produce for her sandwiches at Elliniki Agora, a market a few blocks from the cafe.

Her other expenses are tightly controlled. For example, Brown has lived in the same two-bedroom apartment in Astoria for nearly 30 years. The apartment is rent-stabilized and costs $1,600 a month, a sum she divides with her husband and son.

Brown arrived in New York in the late 1980s. It was a change of pace after spending her childhood in Miami.

She landed a bartending gig in New York, but life in the city wore her down. She seriously considered moving to Hawaii to escape.

Before packing up, she wanted to try acting lessons in New York, the one thing that she could “only do here and nowhere else in the world.” That decision changed her plans. She loved acting and began setting goals for herself. Each time she reached a milestone, she found another reason to stay in New York.

“I’ve had very good years, and when you have a good year, if you’re smart, you invest it or you save it,” she told the Times. “And that’s what I do, because otherwise who knows what’s going to happen next year?

#5308. Nvidia raised next year’s sales target by tens of billions of dollars, signaling confidence in its future without Jensen Huang

Nvidia raised its sales forecast for its next fiscal year, and reported stronger-than-expected results in its most recent quarter, in a striking signal of business confidence by the AI chipmaker following the resignation of longtime CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang.

“Our momentum is real,” interim CEO Colette Kress said on conference call with analysts on Tuesday, citing strong demand for the company’s products, Nvidia’s ongoing technological advances, and the commitment of its employees. Kress, Nvidia’s longtime finance chief, made her debut as interim CEO on Tuesday’s earnings call, flanked by newly appointed chair of the board Harvey Jones.

The pair took pains to project a business-as-usual attitude—even using the phrase—while seeking to put Huang in the rear-view mirror. The board of directors “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said at the start of the call, noting that the company has retained executive recruiting firm Hedrick & Struggles to search for a permanent CEO.

The comments were a direct rebuttal to Huang, who is seeking to reclaim the CEO throne just days after resigning amid revelations of multiple affairs, one reportedly with a Nvidia employee and another with a woman some believe may be a Chinese spy.

Shares of Nvidia were up more than 5% in after hours trading on Tuesday. The company’s stock has plummeted more than 36% in the past month, shedding more than a trillion dollars in market value.

Investors have been spooked by the loss of Nvidia’s longtime leader, Huang, as well as by general concerns about the durability of the AI boom. Kress doused both concerns at once on Tuesday by raising sales expectations for Nvidia’s fiscal 2028 year, which is roughly equivalent to the 2027 calendar year.

“We had originally indicated that we would be at about 70% growth year-over-year, and now we are are increasing that to 75%” growth,” Kress said, citing improvements in supply and ongoing strength in demand. The guidance was particularly striking. because Huang himself had delivered the 70% growth forecast three months ago, framing it as an usually far-reaching forecast that reflected the exceptional strength in the business.

In raising the annual revenue forecast by the equivalent of $20 billion or more, Nvidia’s message seemed to be that Huang was not so essential after all. “We got this,” Kress said during the call.

Revenue in three months ended October 25 totaled $115.8 billion, roughly twice the amount it generated in the year ago period, and above the $109 billion expected by analysts. Net income increased 105% to $65.3 billion, or $2.70 per share. The world’s leading maker of AI chips said it expects revenue in the fourth quarter to come in at $130 billion, plus or minus 3%—besting the $125 billion expected by analysts at the low point and potentially exceeding the target by billions of dollars.

Nvidia said it would file its official 10-Q report with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission in “the coming weeks,” rather than on the same day as its earnings announcement as it traditionally has done.

“The quarter answers the first question the market had about Nvidia without its founder: demand did not leave with him,” Dan Ives, a partner and analyst at Yorkville Ives, wrote in a note to investors on Tuesday.

Jensen Huang’s affaire with Alice Huang (no relation) a former executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed has raised questions about whether Nvidia’s advanced AI chips were being diverted to China, in violation of U.S. export controls. On Monday, U.S. Department of Justice announced that it was pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed for potential export control violations. The Trump administration also announced stricter rules Monday around chip exports to companies like Megaspeed. (Megaspeed has said its business is “legitimate and lawful,” and that Alice Huang, who some U.S. intelligence officials reportedly believe is connected to Chinese intelligence, left the company in August 2025).

Kress said the company was in the process of assessing the new rules around chip exports, but stressed that the company remained confident of overall demand and of its revenue forecast.

Alexei Oreskovic is the Tech editor at Fortune.

#5307. Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 2:31 pm

Update, Tuesday Nov. 17: ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff. Read our follow-up story for details. This story has been updated with ULA’s preliminary findings.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit Sunday, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased.

ULA said Sunday that it didn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it would work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as quickly as possible.

Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to reach orbit. The Centaur, powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris, appears to have started normally and couldn’t make up for the shortfall. ULA appears to have lost telemetry and the mission about 10 minutes into the flight.

Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t said what caused the shortfall.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security launches after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the New Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported.

ULA is also under new leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

#5306. Posting on LinkedIn Got Me One Big Client. What I Did Next on the Platform Built the Rest of My Business.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Posting on LinkedIn gets you seen, but the step most leaders skip is what builds relationships that lead to bigger opportunities.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’ve been a licensed therapist in private practice for almost 15 years. In 2020, I started doing executive psychology coaching, and I changed my content on LinkedIn to reflect that.

My first big paying coaching gig didn’t come from someone I reached out to. Someone saw my content on LinkedIn and asked if I would like to interview and potentially coach their CEO. I ended up coaching that CEO for a few years.

That client found me because I was visible. But almost everything that’s come since then came from something most leaders skip on LinkedIn: reaching out.

I kind of fell into executive coaching. The more I worked with leaders and high achievers on their own inner world, the more their businesses grew. So I didn’t keep posting about my therapy practice. I started posting about the psychology of leadership — things like mental health in leadership, communication, interpersonal relationships, emotional intelligence and the neuroscience behind all of it.

I wanted to help leaders understand their brain and what’s working and not working around their success. There are a lot of executive coaches out there — there aren’t a lot of executive psychology coaches. So I wrote from that angle.

I was posting about three times a week, and it took maybe nine to 12 months before anything came of it. That’s a long time to keep posting when nothing is coming back. If you’re just starting, expect that. Keep doing the work anyway, and post about what you want to be known for. But posting is only half of it.

In my work, I talk a lot about how we don’t have problems; we have patterns. One I see over and over in high achievers is “it’s just easier if I do it myself.” On LinkedIn, that pattern looks like posting and logging off. You share your thoughts, you check the likes and you move on. You don’t send the message. You don’t ask for the introduction. You don’t let anyone help you.

Posting feels safe because you’re in control of it. Reaching out means someone might not answer. For a lot of high achievers, that’s harder than it sounds.

I’ve had people I became friends with on LinkedIn for about 10 years. Some of them I’ve met in person now. Some of them I’ve done speaking events with. We make introductions for each other, and those introductions have led to bigger opportunities.

One of my big LinkedIn connections helped me with my TEDx talk. Another one had me on their podcast. We became friends, and going on that show grew my following significantly.

Then a producer saw me on LinkedIn and reached out about being part of a reality docuseries. I said yes, and during production, I met some amazing entrepreneurs who are still good friends of mine. Some of those connections later introduced me to writing for Entrepreneur.

I have close to 30,000 followers on Instagram. But I’ve gotten more business from LinkedIn than from any other social media platform I’ve ever been on, because of the professional relationships built there. One relationship led to another, and then another.

Start by seeing who’s already looking at you. For me, that’s the most useful part of LinkedIn Premium Business: the analytics. I can see everyone who’s viewed my profile for up to a year — not just the last few people — which turns quiet interest into leads I would have missed otherwise.

If you run a service business, Premium Business also showcases your services and what clients say about you, right on your profile, so people see why to trust you before you ever reach out.

Put the two together, and your outreach is never cold. Whether someone checked out your profile or commented on your post, go see who they are. Send a message, even if you’re not connected yet. Then get on a call. You can also add a custom button that links to your calendar, so it’s easy for people to book that first conversation.

And when a conversation goes well, don’t let it end there. There’s one person I’ve stayed in touch with for the last 10 years. We have a 30-minute call once a month. If we have to skip one, we move the calendar invite instead of canceling, so we never lose that point of contact.

If you’ve connected with someone on LinkedIn and enjoyed the conversation, put something on the calendar. Then keep it there.

That CEO found me because I kept showing up. But the business I have today was built by the people I reached out to after that.

If you’re ready to do more than post and log off, LinkedIn’s new Small Business Playbook shares practical ways to grow your network and turn connections into customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to make your next conversation easier to start.

Relationships are what build businesses, and LinkedIn does a very good job of that if you put in the effort and think about it that way. It’s a group of professionals who are all trying to build their businesses. You’d be surprised how many people actually want to help you. And you want to help them.

I’ve been a licensed therapist in private practice for almost 15 years. In 2020, I started doing executive psychology coaching, and I changed my content on LinkedIn to reflect that.

My first big paying coaching gig didn’t come from someone I reached out to. Someone saw my content on LinkedIn and asked if I would like to interview and potentially coach their CEO. I ended up coaching that CEO for a few years.

That client found me because I was visible. But almost everything that’s come since then came from something most leaders skip on LinkedIn: reaching out.

#5305. ZetaChain's 55M ZETA Burn Isn't a One-Time Event: What Proposal 2 Really Does

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no new mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain says nothing moves unless it passes.

If it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's new private AI app, ZetaLabs, launches alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a new whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

The snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the plan, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain says it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain says the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange users depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

On the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain says it will announce any change to the process in advance.

The vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

If it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Taken together, this looks more like a retirement plan for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

#5304. Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am

It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”

Instead, the Copilot as “a new OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

Microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

The high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

Operating systems like Windows provide users with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the new Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

The New OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

Currently, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the new Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as New OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

If you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, users don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

“We increasingly think of all our apps together as a new operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” said Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

The end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella said.

The Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.
