The first line of code for the core of what would become the XRP Ledger (XRPL) was written about 15 years ago, on November 11, 2011, by David Schwartz.

According to the official XRP account on X, the date 11/11/11 marked the beginning of Schwartz's work on what would later support one of the cryptocurrency industry's established payment-focused blockchain networks.

Schwartz, now Ripple CTO Emeritus, was one of three engineers, alongside Jed McCaleb and Arthur Britto, who began developing the XRP Ledger in 2011. The three were inspired by Bitcoin to build an alternative that would address some of its problems, especially in the areas of sustainability and payments.

In June 2012, the XRP Ledger went live. Shortly after Chris Larsen joined the group in September 2012, a company called NewCoin was formed; it soon changed its name to OpenCoin before becoming Ripple. The founders of the XRPL donated 80 billion XRP, the network’s native digital asset, to the company.

Ripple has locked up most of its XRP in escrow, about 55 billion XRP, and releases 1 billion XRP on the first day of every month.

The anniversary on November 11 marks the start of the XRP Ledger’s development, as what began with Schwartz's first code in 2011 eventually morphed into a blockchain network designed to enable value transfers.

November is also a big month for XRP as U.S. spot XRP ETFs celebrate the first anniversary of their landmark launch.Canary Capital’s XRP exchange-traded fund, listed under the ticker XRPC, began trading on November 13, 2025, and is the first spot XRP ETF on a U.S. exchange.

In upgrade news, XRPL version 3.5.0 is scheduled for December 3, 2026. This release includes only improvements and fixes, including a permanent fix for occasional slow ledger close times.

#5237. OpenAI acquires Odessia, travel startup created by Sonder founder

OpenAI has acquired an AI travel agent called Odessia, according to Odessia’s founder, Francis Davidson. Davidson says in a post announcing the deal that he’s now working for OpenAI, helping the AI lab with the future of travel.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but this looks like an acqui-hire. Davidson’s announcement focused largely on how he built his AI travel agent Odessia by directing teams of AI agents. The year-old Odessia raised a $6 million pre-seed round led by Sequoia and launched its AI travel agent around five months ago. Davidson says that it had helped early adopters plan millions of dollars’ worth of travel, but the tool has already been shut down.

An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed the hire to TechCrunch. “We’re thrilled to welcome Francis to OpenAI. Francis is a proven founder who has built multiple businesses to help people travel, and we’re excited he’s chosen to build with us.”

However the AI lab has not announced new travel-specific products or plans. It does, however, count such companies as Bookings.com, Expedia, and KAYAK as customers or partners. Travel is also one of the main areas that people are using personal AI assistants to help with. And, back in July 2025, when OpenAI launched its ChatGPT agent, it mentioned travel as one of its potential uses.

OpenAI’s spokesperson didn’t have more to share on its plans for travel-related products, except to say that travel is one of the areas that chatbot users frequently ask about. “1.2 billion people turn to ChatGPT each week for help with everyday tasks — from understanding their health, figuring out what to make for dinner, building a budget, and even planning a trip. We see a real opportunity to make these experiences even more useful,” the spokesperson said.

Acquiring Odessia is interesting for another reason. Davidson is well known in the travel industry after he founded a travel startup called Sonder as a college student in 2014. It was sort of like Airbnb, but it focused on short-term leasing of upscale apartments in major cities worldwide. The pandemic badly hurt it, and as it climbed out of that rut, it went public via a SPAC but didn’t raise as much money as it needed, Davidson later said in a post announcing his resignation as CEO in June 2025.

When a key partnership with Marriott fell through, the company went into bankruptcy and wound down. The bankruptcy trustee sold Sonder’s name, trademarks, and website domain in 2026 to TravelAI, and that website operates as a curated guide to the kind of travel rental properties that Sonder was once known for. Prior to its downfall, Davidson had built Sonder into a unicorn with over $600 million in revenues. While Sonder was not, ultimately, a success story, Davidson is the kind of battle-scarred founder that Silicon Valley often values.

So we’ll have to wait and see what OpenAI has in store with travel now that he’s joined the company.

#5235. With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips

Fractile, a British startup developing AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C backed by Britain’s Sovereign AI Fund with hopes of “ensuring the U.K. has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy,” its government stated.

Alongside the likes of Axelera, Etched, and OLIX, this makes Fractile one of the top-funded startup players in the race for purpose-built AI chips. Such chips are one of several avenues being explored to reduce the cost of inference — aka using increasingly demanding AI models in production.

However, Fractile seeks to go beyond hardware with a full-stack approach that also includes a machine learning compiler to maximize the speed at which LLMs will get executed on its chips.

As a result, the company frames itself as a frontier AI company, and its latest round led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Redpoint was priced accordingly. According to the British government, the valuation was “over £5 billion” — quite possibly $7 billion, a figure reported both by the Financial Times and a Reuters source.

Still, Fractile’s main differentiator will arguably be its hardware design. After a pivot, its approach now revolves on DRAM, the most common type of RAM, but stacked on top of each chip in such a way that it is hoping will bypass the usual trade-off between memory and capacity.

This trade-off has become more problematic with the rise of agentic AI, as companies seek to perform longer chains of tasks with large models without compromising on speed. As compute struggles to keep up, hopes are high for AI chips, despite their limited availability to date.

In a LinkedIn post, Fractile CEO Walter Goodwin wrote that “there is still a lot of work ahead” for the company, and that the new funding will enable the startup to “ship [its] first chips and systems next year.”

#5234. PwC’s IPO Lead On A Selective Market, AI Valuations And The Outlook For 2027

The U.S. IPO market has rebounded, but the recovery remains uneven. Companies seeking to go public face investors focused on durable revenue, profitability and valuation, while uncertainty has prompted some issuers to postpone their offerings.

Mike Bellin, a partner and U.S. IPO services leader at PricewaterhouseCoopers, sees a market that remains open to companies with the right scale, financial metrics and preparation.

In a recent conversation with Crunchbase News, Bellin discussed the slowdown in IPO momentum, how public investors are evaluating AI companies, biotech’s resurgence and why SPACs are attracting renewed interest. He also outlined what could set the stage for a stronger start to 2027.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Crunchbase News: How healthy is the IPO market right now?

Bellin: A good IPO year in the U.S. is anywhere from 125 to 175 traditional IPOs, and year to date we’ve seen just south of 90 or so.

The breadth of the market shows me that it’s been a healthy market. We’ve seen industrial products come back to market. We’ve seen tech, consumer markets, energy, utilities and some financial services come back to market.

For the majority of the first three quarters of the year, it was a pretty strong and broad IPO market. But the momentum has halted significantly since September and October.

Is the market in trouble? I would say no. It’s very selective. It’s not shut. Quality issuers with readiness, the right story, the right metrics can still get their deals done.

Bellin: The macro environment in general was the big mover: rates, inflation, geopolitical concerns. Just that uncertainty was a big factor.

One of the big factors that I’ve seen is valuation. Some fairly aggressive valuations were being asked for in certain transactions, certain offerings, and I think the market — with all those uncertainties that I mentioned — was looking at those valuations and thinking it was maybe a bit rich.

I believe many issuers decided to hit pause and wait for another window to open.

What are public market investors looking for?

Bellin: What investors are really looking for is durable revenue — revenue that’s backed up by strong customers, diverse customers and a growing revenue base. I think it’s that revenue reliability where there is a significant backlog of demand for the product, the services of the IPO issuer. That’s always a strong sign.

The other item is leverage. For companies with significant leverage in a rising-rate environment, the questions are: Can they take on new leverage that creates profitable value opportunities going forward? Can they refinance existing leverage given rates are higher?

Making sure that you’re going into the capital markets with a reasonable leverage ratio, or explaining through your equity story how you’re getting a return on the capital that you have invested from a debt perspective, makes a significant difference.

Is the market open to a broad range of venture-backed startups, or primarily larger companies?

Bellin: Scale matters. Companies that have that scale, whether it’s from a revenue perspective or an asset-based perspective, depending on the sector, make a big difference. Those are the types of companies that can almost dictate the window that they’re going to go out in and do well.

Some of the smaller companies, the midmarket companies, smaller-cap companies — again, outside of life science and biotechs — they’ve been a little bit challenged.

If you’re growing at the right rate, you’re showing the right metrics, the IPO market is fully available to those types of companies. But if you’re still on the lower-scale side of the house, your opportunities may be limited to hit the market.

Will enthusiasm for AI companies carry into public markets, or will investors be more skeptical?

Bellin: I think investors aren’t skeptical of AI; they’re skeptical of spend without visibility — visibility to future earnings, visibility to that revenue durability that I mentioned.

The market is separating AI companies with visible demand from the ones with only a narrative out there, and I think that demand, that growth, the backlog is key.

The other factor we’re seeing in today’s market again comes down to cash generation and profitability. If you’re not profitable, when will that profitable period come? Profitability comes in many different measures. Could be GAAP income, could be EBITDA income, but also cash flows and free cash flows and levered free cash flows that are available to the company.

We haven’t seen a period like this of development, of growth, ever before. It’s exciting, but I do think the market will discern between those companies that are public-company worthy and those that are not.

What does the uneven performance of newly public companies signal?

Bellin: It signals selectivity. There have been some really big winners in the IPO market, and others that, post-issuance, haven’t traded as well as many expected.

Many of the companies that are coming to market have to be very thoughtful on the valuation and what you’re going to go price at. If you’re trying to be too aggressive on pricing, you may trade down post-IPO, which is going to impact those metrics.

Overall, we’re seeing strong candidates come to market. I do think companies are coming to market better prepared now than ever, given this volatility.

Bellin: The M&A market for many of these companies is very strong today. As some of the larger health company names lose the patents to some of the profitable drugs, they’re looking at that next generation of development and where there could be value.

Many of these biotechs were purchased by large pharma companies even before coming to the public markets. That competition for these assets and companies is creating a nice horse trade between an IPO opportunity with a lot of upside and an M&A exit with more certainty day one.

I think M&A is the engine behind the IPO market’s resurgence for these companies.

In the IPO markets, many of these assets have traded very well, and that’s where the momentum and that flywheel effect in the IPO market is very important. We’ve seen that flywheel and that momentum in biotech. We haven’t seen it in the rest of the market in the last couple of months.

Why are SPACs attracting renewed interest?

Bellin: With market volatility, we’re seeing more conversations around SPACs. Because SPACs set valuation certainty on day one, a company looking to exit via SPAC understands the potential cash that may come their way. It’s not certain, of course, given redemptions, etc.

Another factor driving a healthy SPAC market may be these serial SPAC issuers. They understand the SPAC product. They understand what makes a good de-SPAC candidate, and they know whether the target company can be ready, show growth and hit the milestones that may be discussed in the offering document.

The market is healthier and more mature today than in the past. That said, we’re still seeing many SPACs continue to look for a target, given the massive SPAC inventory available to target companies.

Bellin: Hundreds of companies are in the pipeline, and they’re ready to go when the market is. Much of the remainder of ’26, and the start of 2027, depends on market momentum.

I’m an eternal optimist. There’s a lot of demand on the buy side; there’s still significant capital available to the right companies. So if we can create that momentum here in the remaining months of 2026, I think we’re going to see a strong start to 2027.

The AI ecosystem that we’ve been talking about is healthy. Demand for energy is always significant, and the right energy companies are coming to market. Consumer and industrial products — those are coming back.

Private equity has been very active in ’26, and I’d expect them to continue that activity in 2027.

I think we’re in for a strong year, but it will remain selective.

#5233. Hackers Hijack 178 Major Websites, Including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, and Ledger

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Hackers have turned some of the world’s most recognizable websites into potential crypto theft traps after compromising a third-party platform used by 178 major organizations. The attack injected malicious JavaScript through Optimizely, a website experimentation platform trusted by companies including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, Salesforce, IKEA, and crypto hardware wallet maker Ledger.

Visitors could unknowingly load malware simply by opening an affected webpage, and the consequences go far beyond stolen browsing data. The malicious code can replace crypto wallet addresses copied to the clipboard, redirecting payments straight into attackers’ wallets. Security researchers have already identified $7,040 in crypto received by wallets linked to the campaign.

🚨 BREAKING: Ledger and 177 other major organizations, including Zoom, CNN, and Salesforce, were affected by a massive JavaScript attack.The malware stole cryptocurrency, payment card details, and user data, while also targeting iPhones with exploit kits.

The investigation by cybersecurity firm Report URI identified 188 infected JavaScript snippets belonging to 178 organizations after examining 1,611 Optimizely scripts. The malware operated through trusted website infrastructure, making the attack particularly dangerous. Rather than breaking into every company’s servers individually, attackers injected malicious code into Optimizely customer projects.

Affected websites continued loading JavaScript through Optimizely’s legitimate content delivery network. Visitors had little reason to suspect that a familiar website was serving malicious instructions. This is a dangerous clipboard hijacking mechanism.

The malware searched webpages for crypto wallet addresses and replaced legitimate destinations with addresses controlled by attackers. It could also intercept copied addresses, meaning someone browsing an affected website could potentially paste a fraudulent wallet address elsewhere.

The attack targeted several major crypto networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, TRON, and Litecoin.

A victim could believe they were sending funds to an exchange, another wallet, or a friend. Instead, the transaction could land directly in an attacker’s wallet.

Report URI identified $7,040 in receipts across attacker-controlled wallets by November 16. The funds included Bitcoin, Litecoin, Ethereum, TRON, and stablecoins.

The scale of the incident raises questions about how much trust businesses place in third-party website services. The affected organizations span several industries, including banking, technology, media, retail, and crypto.

HSBC was among the financial institutions affected, alongside Equifax and other major organizations. BBC, CNN, Fox News, Zoom, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, and Air France-KLM also appeared in Report URI’s investigation.

Ledger’s inclusion makes the incident particularly concerning for crypto users. The company is known for its hardware wallets, which help customers store private keys away from internet-connected devices. However, the incident demonstrates how threats can reach users through ordinary browsing activity, outside the hardware wallet itself.

The malicious campaign also contained capabilities targeting Apple devices. Researchers identified exploit infrastructure associated with Coruna and DarkSword, two iOS exploit kits designed to target vulnerabilities in iPhones and iPads.

This means the operation was not limited to stealing crypto or payment information. It also carried tools capable of targeting mobile devices through malicious webpage content.

Optimizely confirmed that attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The company said it blocked access to the vulnerable pathway, deployed a fix, removed injected code, revoked active tokens, and reset access for affected accounts.

Earlier today, Optimizely identified and contained a security incident affecting some Optimizely Web Experimentation customers. The vulnerable path is blocked, the injected code was removed, and customers have been contacted directly. Updates: https://t.co/ptZHZviIeC

However, the incident raises serious questions about third-party website security. Report URI’s investigation found that even Optimizely’s own websites carried the malicious code. Researchers also observed the attacker rebuilding the malware 26 times during the campaign, adding capabilities and additional cryptocurrency wallets.

Most infected snippets were subsequently cleaned up, with Report URI finding only one remaining infected snippet in its final November 16 sweep.

But the financial damage and potential exposure remain difficult to measure. Researchers have identified crypto receipts, but the number of affected visitors, compromised payment cards, and exposed browser sessions remains unknown.

The bigger problem is that website visitors rarely know which third-party scripts are running behind the pages they trust. A familiar banking website, news outlet, or crypto platform can become an unexpected entry point for malicious code without its visitors noticing anything unusual.

Major crypto exchange Coinbase is set to suspend trading in 12 crypto trading pairs as part of an effort to improve overall market health and consolidate liquidity on the platform. This decision affects two trading pairs involving Cardano (ADA) and Stellar (XLM): ADA/ETH and XLM/BTC.

Coinbase said it regularly monitors the markets on its exchange and, in line with this, trading will be suspended on the named markets on November 25, 2026. In an effort to improve overall market health and consolidate liquidity, Coinbase will be removing a number of non-USD trading pairs for supported assets.

According to an announcement, Coinbase will suspend trading on the following markets on November 25, 2026, at or around 12 PM ET: APE-USDT, ATOM-USDT, ALGO-BTC, CRV-BTC, ETC-BTC, ICP-BTC, XLM-BTC, APE-EUR, ADA-ETH, 1INCH-GBP, CHZ-GBP, SNX-GBP.

In light of this, APE-USDT, ATOM-USDT, ALGO-BTC, CRV-BTC, ETC-BTC, ICP-BTC, XLM-BTC, APE-EUR, ADA-ETH, 1INCH-GBP, CHZ-GBP have been moved to limit-only mode on Coinbase Exchange and Coinbase Advanced.

In recent delistings, Coinbase has disabled trading for Balancer (BAL) and Tensor (TNSR), but users will continue to have the ability to withdraw their funds at any time.

The suspension of trading for Stargate Finance (STG) and Vulcan Forged (PYR) has also been postponed to November 20, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET. Based on recent reviews, Coinbase will suspend trading for Ampleforth Governance Token (FORTH) on November 23, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET. Trading for Neon EVM (NEON) and Syndicate (SYND) will be suspended on November 16, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET.

Spot trading for Pearl (PEARL) will go live on November 13, 2026. The opening of the PEARL-USD trading pair will begin at or after 9 AM PT, if liquidity conditions are met, in regions where trading is supported.

Perpetual futures trading for GRAM, GRASS, QNT and ZRO will go live on November 13, 2026, at or after 12:00 PM UTC.

#5231. Nine Korean startups vie for a spot in Disrupt 2027’s Startup Battlefield 200 competition

TechCrunch’s yearly Startup Battlefield 200 competition sees hundreds of companies from across the world trying every year to get a chance to pitch in front of VCs and the international tech community at the TechCrunch Disrupt conference.

This week, nine early-stage South Korean startups pitched at DETO 2026, a technology conference in Seoul, to earn a spot in next year’s Startup Battlefield 200.

The startups work across the deep tech sector, including healthcare, fintech, energy, semiconductors, and AI. All nine startups are looking to enter the U.S. market as part of the broader international expansion plans.

Voinosis, which develops AI to detect changes in brain health through voice analysis, won the competition. The other eight startups are listed below in alphabetical order.

Voinosis is developing an AI tool that analyzes speech patterns such as pitch, pauses, rhythm, and response times to detect changes linked to brain health. Each voice check takes less than five minutes.

The company says its technology has been tested in Greek, Japanese, and English, and its product doesn’t require separate training for each language. In a clinical study involving 146 participants, the startup claims its tech achieved 88% accuracy in screening for potential cognitive issues.

Voinosis targets hospitals, senior living facilities, insurers, and individual consumers. It also plans to link voice checks with cognitive training, assessments, and treatment provided by healthcare professionals.

The startup was founded by Grace Shin, who spent more than 25 years as an otologic surgeon. The startup is currently raising a Series A round and has already secured a South Korean pharmaceutical company as a strategic investor.

Awesome Lab, based in Seoul, makes ThermoFlux, a heating system that uses water electrolysis and ionization to generate heat. The system can manage heat production for buildings, water supply, and industrial processes. The company says its technology can reduce energy consumption and carbon emissions.

For its international expansion, Awesome Lab is taking a different approach in each market. In the U.S., it plans to supply core OEM modules and work with boiler, water heater, and HVAC companies on product development.

Crosshub helps travelers and international visitors verify their identities and set up payment methods abroad. Its platform, IDBlock, combines identity verification and payment services using self-sovereign identity (SSI) and zero-knowledge proof.

The company says its platform helps users prove their identity across borders without sharing unnecessary personal information. Crosshub is also integrating this technology with payment systems to improve access to financial services for travelers.

DeepFusion AI has developed a 4D radar-based imaging system with additional sensors for autonomous mobility, robotaxi, maritime surveillance, and defense applications. The system combines RF sensors with radar and lidar to detect objects, movement, or distance without a direct line of sight. All sensors are supposedly packed into a single, customizable unit.

EFLOW develops special motors that can produce more torque, or rotational force, while taking up less space for use in robots, drones, satellites, and other mobility applications. The startup also develops actuators that control how robotic joints move.

Otiton Medical makes two medical devices: One specializes in measuring body temperature, while another can capture ear canal images and analyze the eardrum. The company says its AI was trained on about 55,000 images of eardrums, and the device has received medical certification in South Korea.

Riibotics says it can deploy robots into warehouses within a day. Riibotics wants to reduce deployment costs for warehouses by streamlining setup, which includes infrastructure setup, warehouse mapping, system integration through custom middleware, task programming, and safety checks.

Ternell, a semiconductor startup based in Ulsan, is developing a new type of memory to help AI chips use less power.

Unlike conventional two-state memory, Ternell’s T-SRAM system adds a third state for more efficient data storage. Founded in 2019 by KyungRok Kim, a former Samsung Electronics engineer, Ternell reports that tests with 28-nanometer chips showed a 33% to 102% increase in memory capacity per area, and a 55% to 71% reduction in energy needed to access data, compared with conventional SRAM.

Testbank is a Korean edtech startup developing Solve, an app that converts printed study materials, such as workbooks and test-prep books, into interactive digital versions.

The startup uses AI to identify question and answer spaces in publishers’ PDF files while preserving the original layout. Solve lets you write answers directly on the page and be graded automatically.

#5230. ACryptoS Loses $665K Across 77 Vaults on Five Chains After a Missing Input Check

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit. Five exploiter addresses have been published.A vault is supposed to hand out shares in proportion to what you put in. ACryptoS's vaults handed out most of the pool for the price of one small token deposit, because a function never checked how many amounts it had been given.

ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains. In its announcement on X, the project blamed a lack of input validation that let an attacker mint the majority of a vault's shares by depositing only a minimal amount of tokens.

It then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, said it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database. It traces the bug to the `depositMulti` function, where the length of the amounts array was never verified against the number of tokens. An attacker could deposit a tiny amount of a single token, receive the vast majority of vault shares and then withdraw a proportional share of both tokens. SlowMist lists the affected chains as Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.

Multi-token vaults, like those behind liquidity-pair strategies, take deposits in more than one asset. A function such as `depositMulti` receives a list of amounts, one for each token the vault holds. The contract then values that bundle against the pool and issues shares accordingly.The safeguard is basic: the number of amounts supplied must equal the number of tokens in the vault. When the two don't match, the contract is working from incomplete or mismatched input, and its valuation logic can behave in ways its authors never intended. According to SlowMist, that check was absent.How ordinary this flaw is deserves a mention. It isn't an oracle trick or a flash-loan puzzle. It's a missing `require` statement on a public function, exactly the kind of slip that audits and fuzzing exist to catch.

A simplified illustration shows how the numbers work. ACryptoS's published analysis doesn't include the exact contract code, so what follows describes the mechanics of this class of bug, not a line-by-line reconstruction.In a healthy vault, shares are minted in proportion to the deposit's share of the pool. Suppose a vault holds $10,000 in assets and has issued 10,000 shares. A $1 deposit should mint about 1 share, or 0.01% of the supply, and redeeming those shares returns about $1.Now let mismatched inputs throw off the mint calculation. The ratio of deposit to pool collapses or inverts, and the contract might credit the attacker with 90,000 new shares for that $1. The attacker then holds 90,000 of 100,000 shares, or 90% of the supply. Because withdrawals pay out pro rata, redeeming those shares returns about 90% of each token in the pool, roughly $9,000, for a $1 deposit.The reported total fits that scale. Spread across 77 vaults, $665,000 averages about $8,600 per vault, which points to relatively small pools drained repeatedly rather than a few large ones. It also explains why the attack could be repeated mechanically: each vault offered the same function and carried the same flaw.

Yield aggregators usually deploy vaults from a shared template, and each vault's strategy contract inherits the same logic. As a result, one unchecked function in that template turns into one exploit multiplied by every deployment. Seventy-seven vaults on five chains is what that multiplication looks like.The setup also keeps the cost of attack low. Once the flaw is understood, a script can walk through every vault on every chain, call the same function and withdraw. On top of that, ACryptoS says the stolen funds have been moved through several cross-chain protocols, a pattern that complicates recovery.

ACryptoS has asked exchanges and bridges to flag five exploiter addresses in a follow-up post on X:

The request targets exit points. With the stolen funds hopping across chains, the places where they are most likely to be cashed out or bridged are the ones best placed to slow the attacker down. These are EVM addresses and the exploit spanned five networks, so anyone investigating should check each address on Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.The rest of the response is blunt. Deposits are disabled and withdrawals remain open, with users urged to pull their assets quickly. ACryptoS cited an inability to keep maintaining the protocol, so further patching is unlikely. Remaining users should assume vault pools may be thin, withdraw while the function still works and revoke token approvals granted to ACryptoS contracts afterward. A 10% bounty is a common offer in situations like this, but whether the attacker responds is unknown, and users shouldn't plan around a recovery.

For developers, the lessons are narrow and testable. Every public function that takes an array should check its length against the data it is supposed to match. Share-minting should be tested against an invariant: the value of shares issued can never exceed the value deposited. The ERC-4626 standard defines how vault share accounting should behave, and fuzz tests built on its rules would likely have flagged this.Sunsetting a protocol needs a plan as well. A deprecated vault that still holds funds and still exposes live deposit functions is an open target. Pausing deposits and migrating balances before the maintainers leave costs little compared with leaving an unmaintained contract holding user money.For users, the story repeats a familiar warning. Small, older yield protocols with shrinking teams are the ones most likely to carry unpatched code. This incident has less to do with a clever attack than with maintenance running out before the code was safe, so the best protection is to treat vault deposits in aging projects as temporary.

#5229. The Money Cleared The Bank. Now The Founder Is The Risk.

The round closes. The announcement goes out. For about a week, everyone is happy. Then the pressure doubles.

The number that used to be a hope is now a promise. The board that used to be patient now has a timeline. And the founder who just finished the hardest sales job of their life is expected to make the best decisions of their life, immediately, on less sleep than they’ve had in months.

I’ve spent 17 years coaching about 1,500 leaders, including venture-backed founders. The pattern repeats often enough that I treat the first 90 days after a raise as a danger window.

Founders don’t get complacent in that window. They get flooded, and most of them won’t say so out loud.

Neuroscientist Amy Arnsten’s review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience puts it plainly: “even quite mild acute uncontrollable stress can cause a rapid and dramatic loss of prefrontal cognitive abilities.” The prefrontal cortex weighs options and holds a plan steady.

Notice the word uncontrollable. After a raise, a founder controls less than the cap table suggests: the hiring market, customer timelines, the board’s expectations. The founder hasn’t become less intelligent. The judgment that built the company is just harder to reach.

Porcelli and Delgado, writing in Psychological Science, stressed volunteers with a hand in ice water then offered them financial gambles. They grew more cautious about potential gains and more willing to gamble on potential losses. It was a lab study, but I see the same shape in a founder six weeks after a Series B: hesitant about the bets that justified the round, and suddenly willing to roll the dice on anything that feels like a threat.

The decisions that go wrong in this window rarely feel reckless. They feel rational, because the nervous system is treating uncertainty like an emergency.

Senior hiring. An investor who advises 20 fast-growing technology startups told me one of the biggest sources of leadership friction he sees is a CEO hiring a head of sales because they know the person. The relationship feels safe, so the offer is generous. Then the results don’t come. Under pressure, familiarity feels like certainty. But knowing someone isn’t the same as knowing they can lead sales at the company’s next stage.

Expansion. Pressure condenses time. The new market planned for month 12 moves to month three. The data didn’t change. Waiting became unbearable. One founder I coached pulled a 12-month expansion into three, bragged about how little sleep he was getting, and did everything himself. The second-market launch was a sloppy, drama-filled disaster. The board brought me in to put him back together and triage the launch. Ask whether the evidence changed or your tolerance for uncertainty did.

Co-founder relationships. Harvard Business School professor Noam Wasserman, who studied 10,000 founders for “The Founder’s Dilemmas,” has put the share of high-potential startups that fail because of co-founder conflict at 65%. One founder withdraws because they’re overwhelmed. The other interprets the silence as distrust. A trauma-informed lens doesn’t treat every disagreement as trauma. It builds enough trust that a disagreement doesn’t become one more emergency.

If you sit on the board, the week the wire clears is when you start paying attention. Composure can mean steadiness. It can also hide exhaustion.

The founders who come through this window well tend to have one person outside the cap table, the org chart and the family they can think out loud with before a decision hardens. Investor Matt Cohen has written here that founders often have no one inside their company to confide in. Founders, who is that person for you right now? If you can’t name one, that’s useful information too.

The capital is in the account. The open question is whether the person deciding how to spend it can still reach the judgment that raised it. Find that out before the first big decision, not after.

Executive coach Kelly Meerbott is principal of YOU – Loud & Clear. Her performance coaching is trauma-informed, neuroscience-backed and somatic. For more than 17 years she has coached roughly 1,500 leaders, including venture-backed founders, Fortune 500 executives, and more than 500 senior military leaders. She was named Top Coach in America in 2025, is a TEDx speaker, and has written for Fast Company, Training Magazine and Hotel Executive. She is based in Narberth, Pennsylvania, and holds Professional Certified Coach and Certified Clinical Trauma Specialist certifications.

#5228. Nvidia Futures Top XRP in Crypto Liquidations as Jensen Huang’s Exit Sparks $2.14 Billion Surge

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

The daily trading volume of the NVDA-USDC perpetual contract on the decentralized exchange Hyperliquid has reached a record $2.14 billion, according to CoinGlass. The contract is provided by the Trade.xyz protocol, and only Bitcoin had higher trading volume on Hyperliquid over the same period.

Nvidia futures also surpassed Ethereum, Solana and XRP in trading volume, and the combined volume of Nvidia derivatives across all tracked crypto exchanges reached $9.51 billion, according to CoinGlass.

The latest surge in trading comes amid the resignation of Jensen Huang, the co-founder of Nvidia and the only CEO in the history of the company. Huang stepped down on Nov. 12 amid an internal investigation, and Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO.

On Nasdaq, the price of NVDA went down by as much as 14% during the day, but the stock later recovered most of the loss and closed at $166.19, down 4.34%.

Sharp price moves cost leveraged traders on crypto exchanges $40.86 million, according to CoinGlass. Of that amount, $26.23 million came from the on-chain ticker XYZ:NVDA, and $14.63 million came from the base NVDA contract. The largest single liquidation on Hyperliquid was a $1.54 million long position.

In the base NVDA contract, $8.87 million in long positions and $5.89 million in short positions were liquidated. During the same period, the price of Nvidia futures on crypto exchanges went up by 5.6% to $171.17.

Liquidations in the NVDA contracts were almost twice as large as those in XRP, where traders lost $20.75 million over the same period. The price of XRP went down by 2.5% to $1.0192, and long positions accounted for 94.5% of XRP liquidations, or $19.6 million.

The liquidations came amid a sell-off across major cryptocurrencies. The price of Bitcoin dropped below $70,000 to $69,450.50, down 5.3% over 24 hours, and Ethereum fell 4.1% to $1,958.71.

#5227. Phota Labs uses AI to turn everyday photos into professional-looking shots

A new iOS app called Phota Labs gives users access to a personal AI photo assistant that turns everyday snapshots into images that look like they were taken by a professional photographer, all while preserving the authenticity of the image.

Rather than giving consumers yet another photo-editing tool, Phota Labs aims to use advances in AI to automate the editing process so it’s easier for anyone to get access to better photos.

The a16z-backed startup was founded by Cecilia Zhang and Zach Xia, who met at Adobe while working on computational photography products, including Project Indigo, Lightroom, and Photoshop.

The duo saw a gap in the editing tools on the market and believed that although editing tools can be powerful for enhancing photos, they aren’t very effective at fixing a photo that wasn’t captured well in the first place. Phota Labs changes that by focusing on fixing the shot itself while preserving the natural appearances of those in the image.

“Phota is your personal photo assistant that can make great photos for any moment you want to keep before you even ask, which means that it’s a very proactive experience,” Zhang told TechCrunch in an interview. “Think of it almost like a photographer or virtual photographer who looks over your camera roll and tries to understand what’s happening and how they could have taken that photo for you on the spot for that scene.”

The idea is to use AI to transform photos, whether that’s turning a wide-angle group photo into a tighter portrait or transforming a selfie into a regular shot.

Users can choose from different photography styles that determine how AI transforms their images, ranging from subtle edits that preserve the original lens and composition to more dramatic transformations that introduce effects like fish-eye lenses, alternative angles, and entirely different perspectives.

While some people turn to ChatGPT and other generative AI tools to enhance or edit images, these tools can often alter a person’s appearance, especially when working with blurry photos because they don’t know what that person actually looks like.

“For Phota, we built our own tech,” Zhang said. ”We built this personalization technology that actually learns about people’s identity and is able to preserve them in any transformation we do to a photo.”

Images edited with Phota Labs feature invisible watermarks that identify them as altered by AI when shared on social platforms.

The startup is initially targeting people who take tons of photos and like to share them on social media, but don’t want to deal with the tedious process of editing photos. Over time, the founders envision a broader audience, from retirees looking to create beautiful photos for their grandchildren to parents who want to share polished family albums with friends and relatives.

“We have this obsession with authenticity,” Xia said. “I think there’s so much value in connecting AI with real moments and making sure those photos are not perfect, in a sense. That’s why we spend a lot of research into understanding personal context, into building this identity model because we want to make sure the photos are authentic. They’re just better photos of the same moment, rather than saying, ‘Oh, this is an AI image’.”

Xia said beta users were excited to see better versions of moments they had actually lived and saw the results as photos of real memories rather than AI-generated images. The founders discovered that users were taking more photos because they knew Phota Labs could enhance them later.

“We’re turning something that’s unusable into something that people want to print,” Zhang said. “People who just love photos but never really got into editing can now experience professional quality that could never have been possible. So, I think that meant so much to us. There’s so many cherished moments for photos, and we really want them to be actually meaningful and something that you can remember.”

In terms of funding, the company raised a $5.6 million seed round led by a16z last year.

Phota Labs is launching as a free app to build an initial user base before exploring a freemium model. The startup also plans to launch an Android app in the future.

#5226. Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands

Nectar, an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results.

Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research.

Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically.

Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN. The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult.

Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords.

Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular.

Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets.

“Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being said in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.”

Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a new baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals.

Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers.

The company plans to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents.

This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic.

#5224. Genesis AI Raises $500M At $3.5B Valuation To Bring Its Robots To Factories And Warehouses

Genesis AI, a startup teaching robots to perform physical tasks by learning from human movements, announced Tuesday it has raised $500 million in Series A funding at a $3.5 billion valuation.

Premji Invest, Khosla Ventures and Eclipse co-led the round, which brings the company’s disclosed funding to $605 million since its 2024 inception. Genesis previously raised $105 million in a round announced in July 2025.

The company is developing both robots and the AI software that controls them. Its approach combines recordings of human hand movements with training in simulated environments, where robots can practice skills before attempting them in the physical world.

Genesis is initially targeting manufacturing, logistics and laboratories with its robot, Eno.

“We just want to bring something more elegant, more timeless,” co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian told Crunchbase News in an interview. “In the end, this is a very full-stack company. … We have to build all different pieces across the entire stack to make sure we can tightly integrate our technology stack together, and hopefully build the most well-polished and reliable product.

Other participants in the new financing include T. Rowe Price Associates, Durable Capital Partners, Bpifrance, HSG, Nvidia, AMD Ventures, Zoom, Samsung Next and Ericsson. Individual backers include Eric Schmidt, Eric Yuan, Jerry Yang, Xavier Niel and Zach Kirkhorn.

The company plans to use the capital to expand its computing infrastructure, increase robot production and hire more employees, Xian told Crunchbase News. Presently, Genesis has close to 100 employees. It is headquartered in Paris, with offices in San Carlos, California.

Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with most of the investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data.

The closely related field of physical AI has also seen a surge in venture investment this year.

Genesis’s approach grew out of a challenge Xian encountered during his robotics research: The difficulty of finding enough examples for robots to learn from.

Language models have vast amounts of text to draw on. But robots need a different kind of data to learn how to move and for example, pick up and handle objects. They also need that data to better understand what they’re touching and what happens when they act.

Genesis works by using cameras and gloves to capture people’s hand and finger movements as they work, along with touch information. The company says its robotic hand closely matches the human hand and recording glove, making it easier for robots to learn those movements. Historically, collecting this kind of training data involves hiring people to remotely control robots, Xian said. Genesis aims to collect it from people doing their regular jobs instead.

Those recordings help train the company’s AI model, GENE. Genesis also uses its simulation software, Genesis World, to train and test robot skills in virtual environments. The company claims this speeds up a process that would take longer with physical machines alone.

Genesis traces its origins to a research collaboration Xian started in 2022, also named Genesis, while he was pursuing a robotics Ph.D. at Carnegie Mellon University. The project brought together researchers from more than a dozen universities to develop robotics simulation tools.

After graduating at the end of 2024, Xian teamed up with Theophile Gervet and decided to start a company. Genesis formally launched in March 2025 and expanded beyond simulation into AI software and robot hardware.

Xian said developing those components together would help Genesis make them work reliably as a finished product.

“That requires the intelligence, hardware and everything that goes into training and testing the robots to work as one system,” he said.

Genesis is exploring a rental model in which customers would pay for the robot and its software as a combined service. It has announced a partnership with LG CNS and has other Fortune 500 companies in its prospective customer pipeline, according to Xian. He declined to disclose revenue and did not provide a paying customer count.

Premji Invest partner Vedant Agrawal said in a release that the firm was drawn to demonstrations of robots completing extended tasks independently.

“Completing full tasks in real time, not just short clips, is what turns a robot into something a business can rely on,” he said.

Genesis says it is ramping up Eno production for industrial customers. Looking ahead, it plans to expand into hospitality and healthcare, then consumer and outdoor uses.

#5223. AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation

Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday.

That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago, led by IVP.

LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.

With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.

True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well (case in point is newcomer Mintive). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.

#5221. Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say

It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.

Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.

“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.

Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.

Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.

“She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”

Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.

For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal.

“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”

It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.

If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)

Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.

While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.

Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.

Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.

“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.

Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.

Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”

Nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5. According to Artificial Analysis's evaluation, published November 5, that matches Qwen3.8 27B at its xhigh reasoning setting. The model is open weights under Apache 2.0, accepts text only, and has a 524K-token context window.

Behind the tie sits a gap in effort. Artificial Analysis says Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task against 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more. That weighted average covers answer and reasoning tokens across all nine v5 evaluations, including agentic tool-use turns. For anyone running these models, tokens translate into time, electricity or money, so the same score doesn't mean the same cost.

The Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations, among them AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0 and AA-Omniscience. A score of 20 puts Nanbeige well above the 6 of Muse Glimmer, a 30B model in the same comparison. Artificial Analysis also notes that Nanbeige sets a new Pareto-optimal point for Intelligence Index against total parameters, since both it and Qwen3.8 27B are dense models. A larger mixture-of-experts model like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, by contrast, scores 33 while activating only 16B parameters per token.

The model card Nanbeige's lab published on Hugging Face describes the base model, positioned as the flagship teacher for the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab says it will distill agentic capabilities into smaller models, such as an upcoming 3B version. On base-model benchmarks, the card shows 66.9 on MMLU-Pro against 59.3 for Gemma4-31B-Base. Those figures belong to the base model and are separate from the reasoning model's Intelligence Index result.

The two models reach 20 by different routes. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 6% for Qwen, and 16% on the CritPt v2 Hard Subset against 4%. It also edges Qwen on AutomationBench-AA, 53% to 48%.

Elsewhere, it falls behind. On AA-Briefcase v1.1 it scores 1162 Elo against 1391, on FrontierCode 2.0 11% against 15%, and on HLE-Diamond 7% against 15%. The knowledge test tells the most distinctive story. On AA-Omniscience v1.1, Nanbeige scores -4 against Qwen's -6, with an 18% hallucination rate against 29%. Yet it answers only 29% of questions against 43%, declines 71% of them and gets 12% correct against 17%.

For general question answering, Qwen's higher accuracy is the better result.

Output tokens aren't a vanity metric. A reasoning model writes out its thinking as tokens, and every one costs decode time. If both models ran at the same speed on the same hardware, Nanbeige would take about 44% longer to finish a typical task.

Local decoding adds a second factor. Generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, because each new token requires reading the model's weights, and a 33B dense model reads about 20% more weight data per token than a 27B dense model. Assuming the same quantization and the same memory-bound hardware, those two effects compound to roughly 1.7 times the wall-clock time per task. That figure is a back-of-the-envelope calculation, not a measured result.

Nor is there a hosted alternative to soften the blow. Artificial Analysis lists no confirmed public first-party or third-party APIs for Nanbeige, so unlike Qwen, which is sold per token through Alibaba's API, the cost is the hardware you run it on and the time it takes.

Artificial Analysis describes the model as small enough to run locally on a laptop, which holds true with a caveat. The weights are published in BF16, which at 33 billion parameters means roughly 66 GB, far beyond almost any laptop. At 8-bit, the weights fall to about 33 GB, and at 4-bit to about 17 GB, plus memory for the context cache. A machine with 24 GB of unified memory or more can plausibly hold a 4-bit build, though a long context will push it.

The vendor's own quickstart points the other way. The card's SGLang and vLLM examples both set tensor parallelism across four GPUs, which suggests the reference deployment is a multi-GPU server. Its Transformers example also enables trust_remote_code=True, which runs code from the repository. Reading that code first is the safer move, as is serving the model through vLLM or SGLang instead.

Quantization changes the model, too. The Intelligence Index numbers come from Artificial Analysis's own runs, so a 4-bit local build may score somewhat lower, or generate different token counts, than the version they evaluated.

This release is a clean example of why a headline score isn't enough. Nanbeige delivers Qwen-level results at 33B, with strengths in terminal tasks and physics reasoning and a more cautious answering style. The price for those strengths is length.

Anyone choosing between the two should run both on their own workload and record three numbers: the score on their tasks, output tokens per task and seconds per task on their hardware. For terminal-heavy, agentic work, Nanbeige's profile may justify the longer runs. For knowledge-heavy or latency-sensitive work, Qwen's shorter, more accurate answers look stronger.

Three signals are worth watching next: whether the 3B distilled version keeps the model's strengths, whether other labs report the same token behavior, and whether anyone publishes quantized local benchmarks. Until then, the simplest summary is also the most accurate: same score, different bill.

#5218. Flaming Hydra’s new Kickstarter campaign rethinks e-book ownership and digital lending

Here’s a big promise: A new Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.”

That’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project, an initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra. If you back The Phoenix Project, you’re supporting three things — a one-off print magazine designed to celebrate “the values and fun of the early internet,” a new e-book service for libraries, and a newsletter subscription/archiving program that’s also designed for libraries.

To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor, Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.”

Bustillos told me that these issues have been highlighted on Flaming Hydra itself — for example, when Tal Lavin wrote about finding countless AI-generated clones of his book on Amazon. By “creating an ecosystem that is based in people working together, who are offering their stuff in a context that is controlled and doesn’t allow” others to create and sell AI-generated clones, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra is “part of the human project.”

“AI is not this unstoppable force,” she added. “If people just set up publishing pipelines and networks and organizations that are dedicated to the human internet, people who want to read stuff can go to them, and it’s actually completely isolated from mechanistic interference.”

The Phoenix Project fits into this vision by making the work of human writers more accessible to libraries.

Back in 2020, Bustillos wrote about the e-book systems dominating libraries and schools. In one example, instead of just buying a book, a school had to pay $27 per student per year for continued access to copies of “The Diary of Anne Frank.”

This is symptomatic of a broader system that treats true ownership of e-books and other digital media as a thing of the past. Instead, we “license” these e-books from their publishers, and they can be altered or removed at any time.

“E-books are books,” Bustillos said. “They’re not some other thing. They are books, and people should be able to own them, and libraries should be able to own them, and media should be able to be owned. All digital media should be able to be owned.”

In her view, ownership boils down to a simple question: “If you are at the mercy of somebody who can shut the book off, you do not own it.”

So even beyond the question of ongoing payments, there have also been examples of e-books being altered or removed from readers’ devices long after their purchase. Bustillos acknowledged that for individual pieces of media, this distinction may not seem like a big deal, “but if it’s all the textbooks for everybody, if it’s all the books,” then it’s a real problem.

Flaming Hydra and The Phoenix Project seek to solve this by letting libraries truly purchase and own e-books. They can then lend those e-books to their patrons through a new, open source “library in a box” system called Lenny for Libraries.

The Phoenix Project is starting by offering five new e-books from Flaming Hydra writers, including collections of writing from The Awl and of essays by Tom Scocca and Bustillos herself. That might sound like a relatively small start, but Bustillos said she’s talking to library consortiums and author groups, and the goal here is to “change the conversation” around e-books and digital archiving and lending. So The Phoenix Project could be paving the way for other initiatives that follow a similar model.

Similarly, The Phoenix Foundry Archive is designed to make paywalled newsletter content available to libraries. Bustillos noted that “so much of the best journalism, criticism, essays” is now being published in paywalled newsletters that are inaccessible to libraries (as well as the Internet Archive).

Flaming Hydra has been working on all this even before launching the Kickstarter, and Bustillos said she was grateful for the financial support from backers like Anand Ranganathan, Brewster Kahle, and Paul Ford. But by turning to crowdfunding, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra can better protect the work, ensuring that it remains sustainable and independent.

“We don’t have to be at the mercy of anybody, and it also protects editorial independence,” she said. “Those things go hand in hand.”

Flaming Hydra seeks to raise $30,000 for The Phoenix Project, with the campaign ending on November 27.

#5217. Japanese Giant Rakuten Joins Institutional XRP ETF Holders

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Japanese tech and fintech conglomerate Rakuten Group is among the institutional holders of a U.S. spot XRP ETF, according to the company's latest 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Rakuten also holds funds tracking Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana, and these positions were worth roughly $6.42 million combined at the end of the quarter on Sept. 30, 2026.

The filing shows that Rakuten held 6,690 shares of the Bitwise XRP ETF worth $111,255. At press time, the price of XRP stands at $1.03, and the shares of the Bitwise fund trade at $11.51, according to SoSoValue, so the XRP ETF stake of Rakuten is now worth about $77,000.

Rakuten is not the only institutional investor in the new XRP funds, and Raymond James Financial has also disclosed positions in spot XRP ETFs, according to SEC filings.

The largest position of Rakuten is in BlackRock's spot Bitcoin fund, the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF, and Rakuten held $5,893,593 worth of its shares at the end of the third quarter. Besides, Rakuten owns $263,632 of the iShares Ethereum Trust ETF and $150,728 of the Bitwise Solana Staking ETF.

U.S. rules require any institutional manager holding more than $100 million in U.S. exchange-listed securities to disclose its portfolio every quarter, no matter where it's based. Rakuten Group holds about $1.4 billion in U.S. equities, and most of that amount is in shares of satellite operator AST SpaceMobile. In this context, the crypto ETF positions account for less than 0.5% of the U.S. portfolio of Rakuten.

Rakuten is one of the largest tech companies in Japan. The market capitalization of Rakuten stands at about ¥1.4 trillion ($9 billion), and the annual revenue of the company is more than ¥2.5 trillion ($16 billion).

The Rakuten ecosystem spans more than 70 services, from the Rakuten Ichiba marketplace and carrier Rakuten Mobile to banks and brokerages. According to Rakuten, these services have more than 100 million users in Japan and more than 2.1 billion users worldwide.

The latest filing comes amid outflows from spot XRP ETFs. According to SoSoValue, the funds lost $10.42 million on Nov. 9 and another $7.62 million on Nov. 10, and there were no flows on Nov. 11 and Nov. 12. On Oct. 28, the total net assets of the funds stood at $1.51 billion.

Still, the cumulative net inflow of spot XRP ETFs stands at $1.79 billion, and the total net assets of the funds are $1.16 billion, or 1.77% of the market cap of XRP. Finally, the Bitwise XRP ETF is the largest of the five spot XRP funds, and its net assets stand at $420.29 million, according to SoSoValue.

#5216. Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market

Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.

The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.

India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.

The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview.

“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.

Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.

Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.

The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.

The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indusbridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.

Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.

“It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said.

In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.

The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.
